blocks.html: In Introduction to Law you met the schools of statutory interpretation, and in Civics and Government you met judicial restraint and activism. Constitutional law asks a harder version of the same question. The text is short and old, its key phrases are broad ("commerce among the several States," "due process of law"), and a mistake can be fixed only by the Court itself or by an amendment. So what counts as a good argument about what the Constitution means?

In Constitutional Fate (1982) and Constitutional Interpretation (1991), the scholar Philip Bobbitt answered by describing, not prescribing. He read two centuries of opinions and briefs and found six kinds of argument that lawyers and judges accept as legitimate. He called them the modalities of constitutional argument.

head: Modality
It asks
A typical move
rows: Textual
What do the words mean?
"Congress" in the First Amendment names the legislature, so the clause limits lawmaking.
Historical
What did the framers and ratifiers understand?
Quoting the Convention, the ratification debates or the Federalist.
Structural
What follows from how the government is built?
A state cannot tax a federal bank, because one government cannot control another that is supreme in its sphere.
Doctrinal
What do the precedents hold?
Applying a test from an earlier case to new facts.
Prudential
What will the consequences be?
A rule courts cannot administer, or one that would cripple the government in a crisis, is a poor reading.
Ethical
What does the American constitutional ethos value?
Reasoning from limited government or the dignity of the individual.
blocks.cap: Bobbitt's six modalities (our wording and examples).

blocks.html: Every constitutional system needs a way to decide which arguments count. Without one, any outcome could be defended and none could be criticized. The modalities give lawyers a shared grammar: you can disagree with a structural argument, but you cannot dismiss it as "not law." Most strong opinions use several modalities that point the same way, and the hard cases are the ones where they point in different directions.
Constitutional arguments come in six recognized forms: text, history, structure, precedent, consequences and ethos. Name the form before you judge whether the argument is persuasive.

cards.text: "The clause says 'Congress shall make no law,' not 'no government.'"
cards.why: It turns on the words themselves.

cards.text: "Madison told the First Congress the clause was meant to reach only…"
cards.why: It relies on what a framer said at the time.

cards.text: "If states could tax federal offices, the national government would depend on the states it governs."
cards.why: It reasons from the design of the federal system.

"Reading the clause this way would flood the courts and freeze the economy."

blocks.title: Spotting the modalities in McCulloch
blocks.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Chief Justice Marshall upheld the national bank and struck down Maryland's tax on it. Name the modality of each move.
steps: Marshall notes that the Constitution, unlike the Articles of Confederation, does not say "expressly" delegated powers. That is a textual argument (comparing words).
He recalls that the First Congress chartered a bank in 1791 after full debate. That is historical (early practice).
He reasons that a constitution can mark only "great outlines" and must leave the means to Congress. That is structural.
He argues that a state power to tax the bank could destroy a federal institution. That is structural too, with a prudential warning about consequences.
blocks.a: Text, history, structure and consequences, all pointing the same way. That convergence is part of why the opinion has lasted.

blocks.title: Where the modalities split
blocks.q: A state law is challenged. The text of the relevant clause is broad, the founding-era history is thin, and two precedents point in different directions. What does a careful brief do?
steps: Make the textual argument first; it sets the outer bounds.
Add whatever historical evidence exists, and say how strong it is.
Distinguish the unfavorable precedent and show the favorable one fits better (doctrinal).
Close with structure or consequences to show the reading is workable.
blocks.a: It uses several modalities and is candid about which are strong. Judges are persuaded by convergence, and they notice when a brief hides a weak point.

blocks.html: Calling every argument you dislike "just policy." A prudential argument is one recognized form among six, and many weighty opinions use it. Identify which modality an opinion uses first; then ask whether it is strong of its kind. A quick check: could you restate the argument as a claim about words, history, design, precedent, consequences or values? If so, it is a legal argument.

The framers argued in these modes too. Read how Madison reasons from structure in Federalist No. 51, and how Brutus answered with consequences and history. The schools in the next two lessons, originalism and living constitutionalism, are theories about how to rank and combine these modalities.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: Originalism is a family of theories built on one claim: the meaning of each provision of the Constitution was fixed when it was adopted, and judges should apply that fixed meaning. It grew in the 1970s and 1980s through scholars such as Robert Bork and officials such as Attorney General Edwin Meese, and on the Supreme Court through Justices Antonin Scalia and Clarence Thomas, joined later by others. It leans on the textual and historical modalities.

head: Version
What fixes the meaning
Common criticism, and the reply
rows: Original intent
What the framers meant to accomplish
Hundreds of drafters and ratifiers had no single intent. Most originalists moved away from this version for that reason.
Original public meaning (the main version today)
What a reasonable, informed reader understood the words to mean when ratified
Historical meaning can be hard to find. Advocates reply that courts weigh historical evidence all the time, and the method still narrows the choices.
Original expected application
The specific results people expected then
Few originalists hold it: the public meaning of a principle can reach facts the founders never imagined.
blocks.cap: Most originalists today look for public meaning, not private intentions.

blocks.html: Advocates give several reasons. Law, not preference: a written constitution is law because the people ratified its words, and judges have no authority to change them. Restraint: a fixed meaning limits judges, who are unelected and serve for life. Democracy and Article V: if the Constitution needs to change, the people can amend it, as they have 27 times; when judges update it instead, they take that choice from the people. Justice Scalia called his approach the "lesser evil" compared with asking judges to apply their own values.
Originalists hold that a provision's meaning was fixed at ratification, usually as its original public meaning, and that judges must apply that meaning; change comes through amendment.

doc.title: Reading a clause the originalist way
doc.source: U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 8, Clause 3 (1787)
paras: The Congress shall have Power … To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes;

marks.note: An originalist asks how a 1788 reader used "regulate": to prescribe rules for something already going on.
Did "commerce" mean trade and transport only, or all gainful activity? Originalist scholars disagree; the evidence is debated.
In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) Marshall read "among" as "intermingled with," reaching commerce that concerns more states than one.

blocks.cap: Tap the marked words. Originalism turns questions about power into questions about historical meaning.

blocks.title: Public meaning, not private intent
blocks.q: A historian finds a letter in which one delegate wrote that he hoped the Commerce Clause would someday reach manufacturing. A public-meaning originalist is asked whether that settles the clause's meaning.
steps: Private hopes of one drafter are not the meaning the public ratified.
The originalist looks instead for how the word "commerce" was used in dictionaries, newspapers, legal writing and the ratification debates of 1787–1788.
The letter might be weak evidence of usage, but it does not control.
blocks.a: No. Public-meaning originalism asks what the words meant to the ratifying public, not what one framer privately wanted.

blocks.title: Originalism and new technology
blocks.q: Does an originalist have to say that the Fourth Amendment's "papers" and "effects" cannot cover a smartphone, since none existed in 1791?
steps: Separate the fixed meaning of a term from the facts it applies to.
If "effects" publicly meant a person's personal property, a phone is personal property.
The meaning stays fixed; its application reaches new things that fit it.
blocks.a: No. Public-meaning originalists hold that fixed principles apply to new facts. That is the difference from "expected application."

blocks.html: Equating originalism with the framers' private intentions, or with freezing the Constitution in 1788. Most originalists today look to the public meaning of the words when ratified. Check: does the argument rely on dictionaries, usage and the ratification debates (public meaning), or on one framer's hopes (intent)?

Critics answer that history is often unclear, that originalists disagree among themselves, and that the method gives authority to a generation that excluded many Americans from voting. Originalists reply that every method has hard cases, that unclear history calls for deference to legislatures, and that the amendments themselves, such as the Fourteenth, Fifteenth and Nineteenth, were the people's way of correcting the founding. The next lesson presents living constitutionalism as its advocates present it. You can read the founding debates yourself on the ratification debate page.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: Living constitutionalism holds that the Constitution's broad principles are applied to new conditions over time, mostly through precedent built case by case. Its advocates include scholars such as David Strauss (The Living Constitution, 2010) and judges such as Justice William Brennan and Justice Stephen Breyer (Active Liberty, 2005). Like originalism, it is a family of views, and it draws on doctrinal, prudential and ethical modalities as well as text and history.

Advocates give several reasons. This is how our law has in fact developed. Strauss argues that American constitutional law works mostly like the common law: judges reason from precedent, extend it carefully and correct it when experience shows it fails. Much of what everyone accepts today, from the modern commerce power to the law of free speech, grew that way rather than by amendment. The text invites it. The framers wrote some clauses in broad terms ("equal protection," "unreasonable searches") and others in exact ones (a President must be 35). Broad terms, advocates say, state principles meant to be applied by later generations. Amendment is very hard. Article V requires two-thirds of both houses and three-fourths of the states, so a Constitution that could change only by amendment would fall behind a changing country.

doc.title: Marshall on a constitution meant to last
paras: This provision is made in a Constitution intended to endure for ages to come, and consequently to be adapted to the various crises of human affairs.

marks.text: intended to endure for ages to come
marks.note: Living constitutionalists often cite this line for the idea that the Constitution was built to adapt.

marks.text: adapted to the various crises of human affairs
marks.note: Originalists read it more narrowly: Marshall was saying Congress may choose new means to carry out fixed powers, not that the meaning of the Constitution changes.

blocks.cap: One sentence, two readings. Tap the marked phrases.

blocks.html: Living constitutionalists accept the text's authority and read its open-ended phrases as principles whose application develops over time, mainly through precedent; advocates say this is how constitutional law has worked and keeps the Constitution workable.

blocks.title: Principle and application
blocks.q: The Equal Protection Clause (1868) says no state shall "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws." How does a living constitutionalist explain Brown v. Board of Education (1954), which rejected the "separate but equal" rule of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)?
steps: Start with the text: the clause states a general principle of equality, not a list of practices.
Look at experience: decades of cases had shown that "separate" facilities were not equal in fact.
Reason from precedent: cases such as Sweatt v. Painter (1950) had already found separate law schools unequal; Brown extended that line.
Conclude that applying the same principle to new understanding required a different result.
blocks.a: The principle stayed the same; its application changed through case-by-case reasoning. (Many originalists argue that Brown is also right on originalist grounds; the case is not owned by either school.)

blocks.title: The commerce power
blocks.q: In 1895 the Court held that manufacturing was not "commerce"; by 1942 it upheld federal limits on wheat grown for a farm's own use. How would Strauss describe that change?
steps: No amendment changed the Commerce Clause.
The national economy changed, and a long series of decisions, from the narrow era to Wickard v. Filburn, worked out what "commerce among the several States" means in an industrial economy.
That is common-law development: precedent, tested by experience and revised.
blocks.a: As evidence that constitutional law grows through precedent. Critics see the same history as drift from the text; you will judge the cases yourself in the commerce unit.

blocks.html: Thinking living constitutionalists ignore the text. They accept its authority and its exact rules; the disagreement is about broad phrases such as "equal protection" and "due process." Check: does the argument claim the text does not bind, or that a broad principle in the text applies differently to new facts? Only the second is living constitutionalism.

Critics answer that the approach gives judges too much room to write their own views into law, that it weakens the reason for having a written constitution, and that change should come from voters and amendments. Advocates reply that precedent and the craft of judging constrain judges, that originalism leaves just as much room through choices about history, and that common-law growth has served the country well. Practice in this course will ask you to identify each school's arguments, never to choose a winner.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: You learned in Distinguishing and Overruling that courts follow precedent (stare decisis, "to stand by things decided"). Constitutional cases add a twist. If the Court misreads a statute, Congress can pass a new law. If it misreads the Constitution, the only fixes are an amendment, which is rare, or the Court's own correction. So the Court has said that stare decisis is weaker in constitutional cases. Justice Louis Brandeis made the classic statement of this point in 1932: in most matters it matters more that a rule be settled than that it be settled right, but in constitutional cases the Court must be readier to correct itself.

Two values pull against each other. Stability lets people plan, keeps the law from changing with each new justice and shows that the Court decides by law rather than by vote count. Correctness matters too: a wrong constitutional ruling can last for generations if the Court refuses to revisit it. The Court's factors are a way to weigh the two in each case.

Before overruling a constitutional precedent, the Court weighs the quality of its reasoning, its workability, its consistency with related decisions, developments since (changed facts or law) and reliance on it. Stare decisis is "not an inexorable command," and it is at its weakest in constitutional cases.

blocks.title: Applying the factors
blocks.q: A 40-year-old constitutional precedent set a test that lower courts apply in conflicting ways. Later cases have cut back its reasoning. Businesses and governments have arranged contracts around it. List how each factor points.
steps: Quality of reasoning: later cases undercut it, which favors overruling.
Workability: conflicting results below favor overruling.
Consistency: it no longer fits related decisions, which favors overruling.
Reliance: contracts built on it favor keeping it; the Court gives most weight to concrete reliance such as property and contract rights.
blocks.a: Several factors point toward overruling and reliance points the other way. Justices weigh them differently, which is why overruling cases are often closely divided.

blocks.title: Statutory or constitutional?
blocks.q: Why might the Court be slower to overrule its reading of a federal statute than its reading of the Constitution?
steps: For a statute, Congress can correct the Court with an ordinary law.
If Congress has left the reading alone for decades, that silence is some sign it accepts it.
For the Constitution, only an amendment or the Court can correct an error.
blocks.a: Stare decisis is strongest for statutory cases and weakest for constitutional ones.

blocks.html: Thinking the Court rarely overrules itself. It has done so many times, from West Coast Hotel to Janus. Thinking the opposite, that a majority may overrule whenever it disagrees, is also wrong: the factors require a special justification beyond believing the case was wrongly decided. Check both sides of the factor list before predicting a result.

Justices and scholars disagree about how much weight precedent should get. Some originalists argue that a demonstrably wrong reading of the Constitution should yield; others, and many living constitutionalists, treat a long line of precedent as part of the Constitution's meaning. Hamilton expected judges to be "bound down by strict rules and precedents" in Federalist No. 78.

blocks.html: You met judicial review in Civics and Government and learned to brief a case in Introduction to Law. Now read the case that started it all the way a law student does: carefully, and for exactly what it holds.

In the last days of John Adams's presidency in March 1801, the Senate confirmed dozens of new justices of the peace for the District of Columbia. William Marbury was one. His commission was signed and sealed but not delivered before Thomas Jefferson took office, and Jefferson's Secretary of State, James Madison, withheld it. Marbury asked the Supreme Court directly, in its original jurisdiction, for a writ of mandamus ordering Madison to deliver it. He relied on Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, which the Court read as authorizing such writs.

opts.facts: Marbury, appointed a justice of the peace by President Adams, sued Secretary of State Madison in the Supreme Court for a writ of mandamus to deliver his commission.
opts.reasoning: Marshall asked three questions in order: Does Marbury have a right? Do the laws give a remedy? Can this Court issue it? Yes, yes, no: Article III fixes the Court's original jurisdiction, and Congress cannot enlarge it by statute. A law "repugnant to the Constitution is void," and a court deciding a case must apply the Constitution over it.
opts.later: The Court did not hold another act of Congress unconstitutional until Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).

blocks.html: Marshall's argument is mostly structural and textual. The Constitution is written law, "fundamental and paramount." If Congress could change it by ordinary statute, the written limits would mean nothing. Courts decide cases, and "it is emphatically the province and duty of the Judicial Department to say what the law is." When a statute and the Constitution conflict in a case, the court must choose, and it must choose the higher law. Judges also swear an oath to support the Constitution, and Article VI makes laws supreme only if "made in Pursuance" of it.

Marbury v. Madison (1803): Marbury had a right to his commission and a legal remedy, but the Supreme Court could not issue the writ, because the part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that gave it original jurisdiction here was unconstitutional. A court deciding a case must apply the Constitution over a conflicting statute.

blocks.name: cv-order

items: Has Marbury a right to the commission? (Yes)
If so, do the laws give him a remedy? (Yes, mandamus)
Can this Court issue the remedy in this case? (No: Section 13 conflicts with Article III)

blocks.cap: Put Marshall's three questions in the order he answered them.

blocks.title: Why the order of questions mattered
blocks.q: Marshall could have started with jurisdiction and dismissed the case. Why does it matter that he answered the other two questions first?
steps: By finding that Marbury had a right and a remedy, Marshall said the Jefferson administration had acted unlawfully.
By then denying jurisdiction, he gave the administration nothing to defy: the Court ordered nothing.
And by striking down Section 13, the Court claimed the power of judicial review in a case where it gave up power over this dispute.
blocks.a: Historians often describe it as a strategic opinion: it asserted the Court's authority while avoiding a confrontation it might have lost. (Critics note that a court without jurisdiction usually should not reach the merits.)

blocks.title: Finding the holding
blocks.q: A classmate writes: "Marbury held that the Supreme Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution for all three branches." Correct the statement.
steps: Look at what the Court had to decide: whether to apply Section 13 in Marbury's case.
It held that a court may not enforce, in a case before it, a statute that conflicts with the Constitution.
Claims that the Court's readings bind other officials came later, most strongly in Cooper v. Aaron (1958).
blocks.a: Marbury holds that courts must apply the Constitution over a conflicting statute when deciding a case. It does not by itself say the Court is the only or final interpreter.

blocks.html: Thinking Marbury invented judicial review from nothing, or that it made the Court the sole interpreter. State courts and some federal judges had refused to apply unconstitutional laws before 1803, and Hamilton defended the idea in Federalist No. 78: the courts must prefer "the Constitution" to "the statute." The holding itself is narrower than its fame. Check: what did the Court actually do? It declined to exercise jurisdiction a statute gave it.

Not everyone welcomed the power. Brutus warned in 1788 (essays XI to XV) that judges serving for life, whose rulings no one could correct, would read the Constitution by its "spirit," enlarge federal power and stand above the legislature and the people. Read the exchange on the ratification debate page.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: Marbury was about an act of Congress. A harder question for the young country was whether the U.S. Supreme Court could review the decisions of state courts. Section 25 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 said it could, when a state's highest court ruled against a federal claim. Virginia's highest court disagreed.

opts.facts: Virginia had confiscated land that Lord Fairfax left to his nephew, a British subject. The U.S. Supreme Court held in 1813 that a federal treaty protected the title. The Virginia Court of Appeals refused to obey, saying the Supreme Court had no power to review it.
opts.reasoning: Justice Joseph Story wrote that Article III extends the judicial power to all cases arising under federal law, whatever court they start in, and that review of state courts is needed for the "uniformity of decisions throughout the whole United States" on federal questions.

blocks.html: Why must one court have the last word on federal law? Federal law is the same law in every state. Story pointed out that judges "of equal learning and integrity, in different states, might differently interpret a statute, or a treaty of the United States, or even the constitution itself." Without a single reviewing court, the Constitution could mean one thing in Virginia and another in Massachusetts. The Supremacy Clause also binds "the Judges in every State," so state judges apply federal law, subject to review on it.

Five years later, in Cohens v. Virginia (1821), Chief Justice Marshall extended the reasoning to state criminal cases. The principle has held ever since: on a federal question, the U.S. Supreme Court reviews state courts; on a question of the state's own law, the state's highest court is final.

blocks.name: cv-court
blocks.cap: A case that begins in a state court can reach the U.S. Supreme Court only on a question of federal law.

opts.facts: After Brown v. Board of Education, Arkansas's governor and legislature resisted desegregation of Little Rock's Central High School. In 1958 the school board asked to delay its plan for years, citing the turmoil.
opts.reasoning: In an opinion signed by all nine justices, the Court refused the delay. It said the Fourteenth Amendment as interpreted in Brown is part of the "supreme Law of the Land" under Article VI, binding on state officials, who swear an oath to support the Constitution, and that they cannot nullify it.

blocks.html: Martin v. Hunter's Lessee (1816): the U.S. Supreme Court may review state court rulings on federal law. Cooper v. Aaron (1958), unanimous: state officials are bound by the Court's interpretation of the Constitution.

blocks.title: Federal or state question?
blocks.q: Case 1: a state supreme court interprets its own state constitution's education clause. Case 2: the same court rules that a state law does not violate the First Amendment. Which can the U.S. Supreme Court review?
steps: Case 1 turns only on state law. The state's highest court has the last word.
Case 2 decides a federal question. Under Martin, the U.S. Supreme Court may review it.
If a state ruling rests on an adequate and independent state ground, the Supreme Court will not disturb it even if a federal issue is also present.
blocks.a: Only Case 2.

blocks.title: How far does Cooper reach?
blocks.q: Some scholars and officials argue for "departmentalism": each branch interprets the Constitution for its own work. How does that differ from the view in Cooper?
steps: Cooper said the Court's interpretation in Brown was the supreme law, binding state officials beyond the parties to the case.
Departmentalists point to Presidents such as Jefferson, Jackson and Lincoln, who said they owed the Court obedience in a decided case but not agreement in general.
Both sides agree that officials must obey a court judgment in a case; they disagree about whether the Court's reasoning binds everyone else in future matters.
blocks.a: The disagreement is about the reach of the Court's interpretations beyond the judgment. That debate continues; Cooper is the Court's strongest statement of its own supremacy.

blocks.html: Thinking a state supreme court has the last word on federal questions. It has the last word on its own state's law. On federal law the U.S. Supreme Court can review it. Check: which law decides the question? If it is federal, review is possible.

The framers expected this. Federalist No. 80 argues that a federal judiciary is needed for "uniformity in the interpretation of the national laws," and Federalist No. 82 expects state courts to hear federal cases with appeals to the Supreme Court.

blocks.html: Article III creates "one supreme Court" and "such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish." It gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in a few cases (those involving ambassadors and those in which a state is a party) and appellate jurisdiction in the rest, "with such Exceptions, and under such Regulations as the Congress shall make." Those words give Congress real power over the courts. Marbury showed one limit: Congress cannot add to the original jurisdiction.

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: Article III, Section 2, Clause 2: original and appellate jurisdiction, with the Exceptions Clause.

blocks.html: The framers left the lower federal courts to Congress as a compromise: some delegates wanted no lower federal courts at all, trusting state courts to hear federal cases first. Since Congress need not create lower courts, the usual reasoning goes, it may also decide which cases they hear. The Exceptions Clause gives Congress a similar power over the Supreme Court's appellate docket. This is one of the checks Congress holds on the judiciary.

opts.facts: During Reconstruction, the army held William McCardle, a Mississippi newspaper editor, for trial by military commission. He sought habeas corpus under an 1867 law and appealed to the Supreme Court. After argument, Congress repealed the part of the 1867 law that allowed such appeals (March 27, 1868).
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Chase wrote that the Court's appellate jurisdiction is conferred "with such exceptions" as Congress makes. Without jurisdiction the Court could only announce that fact and dismiss. The opinion noted that the repeal did not take away the Court's other habeas jurisdiction under the Judiciary Act of 1789.
opts.later: In Ex parte Yerger (1869) the Court heard a similar prisoner's habeas case through that older route.

blocks.html: Congress may make exceptions to the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction and may create, shape or not create lower federal courts; Ex parte McCardle (1869) accepted a repeal that ended a pending appeal. How far the power goes, for example whether Congress could close every court to a constitutional claim, is debated.

head: View
Main argument
rows: Broad congressional power
The text says "such Exceptions" without limits, and McCardle accepted a repeal aimed at a pending case. Jurisdiction rules are how a democracy checks unelected judges.
Internal limits
An "exception" cannot swallow the rule; the Supreme Court's "essential functions" (uniformity and supremacy of federal law) must survive.
External limits
Other parts of the Constitution still apply: Congress cannot strip jurisdiction in a way that violates due process or equal protection, or that tells courts how to decide a pending case.
blocks.cap: Scholars' views on the outer limits (the Court has not settled them).

blocks.title: Reading McCardle closely
blocks.q: Did McCardle leave detained people with no route to the Supreme Court?
steps: The 1868 law repealed only the appeal route created in 1867.
The Court said its jurisdiction under the 1789 Act remained.
In Yerger (1869) it used that route.
blocks.a: No. That is one reason some scholars read McCardle narrowly: Congress closed one door, not all of them.

blocks.title: A hypothetical
blocks.q: Congress passes a law: "No federal court shall hear any challenge to Statute X." Lay out the arguments.
steps: For validity: Article III lets Congress make exceptions and decline to create lower courts; state courts remain open to hear the claim, subject to the Supremacy Clause.

Against: if state courts are also closed, people could be left with no court for a constitutional right, raising due process concerns; and an exception aimed at one statute's challengers may look like dictating the result.
The Court has not decided a case that squarely tests these limits.
blocks.a: A law that removes only federal jurisdiction, leaving state courts open, is on firmer ground than one that leaves no court at all. The outer limits remain debated.

blocks.html: Thinking Congress cannot touch the Court's jurisdiction. The Exceptions Clause gives Congress real power, and Congress regularly sets jurisdiction by statute (amount-in-controversy rules, for example). Check: is the question whether Congress has any power here (it does) or how far it goes (debated)?

Hamilton addressed this in Federalist No. 81, where he argued that the Exceptions Clause lets Congress make reasonable adjustments to appellate review. Brutus, on the other side, feared courts that could not be checked at all.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: You learned the three parts of standing in Standing: an injury in fact (concrete and particularized, actual or imminent), causation (fairly traceable to the defendant) and redressability (a court order can help), from Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992). Constitutional claims face the same test. One recurring question: can you sue just because you are a taxpayer who objects to how federal money is spent?

opts.name: Frothingham v. Mellon
opts.facts: A taxpayer challenged a federal grant program for maternal and infant health, arguing it exceeded Congress's powers and would raise her taxes.
opts.q: Does a federal taxpayer have standing to challenge federal spending?
opts.holding: No. Her interest in the Treasury was shared with millions of others and was "comparatively minute and indeterminate"; she showed no direct injury of her own.

blocks.html: Why the general rule? Standing keeps courts deciding concrete disputes, not general complaints about government. Every taxpayer funds every program. If any taxpayer could challenge any spending, courts would review the whole federal budget at the request of anyone who disagreed with it, which is the job of Congress and voters. The case or controversy requirement of Article III exists to prevent that.

opts.name: Flast v. Cohen
opts.facts: Taxpayers challenged federal education funds used for instruction and materials in religious schools under the Establishment Clause.
opts.holding: Taxpayers had standing because of a two-part "nexus": (1) they challenged an exercise of Congress's taxing and spending power under Article I, Section 8, and (2) the challenge rested on a specific limit on that power. The Establishment Clause is such a limit.
opts.later: The Court has refused to extend Flast beyond the Establishment Clause, and Hein v. Freedom From Religion Foundation (2007) confined it to spending specifically authorized by Congress.

blocks.html: Federal taxpayers generally lack standing to challenge federal spending (Frothingham, 1923). The narrow exception: an Establishment Clause challenge to congressional spending (Flast v. Cohen, 1968). Hein (2007) refused to extend it to executive spending from general appropriations.

blocks.title: Applying Flast's nexus test
blocks.q: A taxpayer challenges a statute appropriating funds to a program, arguing it violates the Tenth Amendment. Does Flast apply?
steps: Part one: the challenge targets congressional spending under Article I, Section 8. Satisfied.
Part two: the claim must rest on a specific constitutional limit on the taxing and spending power. The Court has said the Tenth Amendment is not that kind of limit.
So the taxpayer fails part two.
blocks.a: No standing under Flast. The Establishment Clause is the only limit the Court has accepted for this exception.

blocks.title: Hein's line
blocks.q: Why did Hein (2007) find no standing for taxpayers challenging the White House faith-based initiative's conferences?
steps: The money came from general appropriations to the executive branch, not from a statute directing it to religious uses.
The plurality (three justices) held Flast's exception covers only expenditures Congress specifically authorized; two more justices concurred in the judgment and would have overruled Flast.
Four dissenters saw no principled difference between congressional and executive spending.
blocks.a: No standing, 5 to 4 in the judgment, with no single majority rationale.

blocks.html: Thinking being a taxpayer gives you standing to challenge any federal spending. The general rule is no. Flast is a narrow exception for Establishment Clause challenges to congressional spending. Check: is there a personal injury beyond being a taxpayer? If not, does the case fit Flast exactly?

Standing doctrine reflects the separation of powers: the courts decide cases, and broad policy disputes go to Congress and the voters. That idea traces back to Article III's words "Cases" and "Controversies" and to Federalist No. 78's picture of a judiciary that acts only through judgment.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: In The Political Question Doctrine you met the idea that some constitutional questions belong to the political branches, not the courts. Standing asks whether this plaintiff may sue; the political question doctrine asks whether this issue is one a court can decide at all. Three cases show how it works.

opts.facts: Tennessee had not redrawn its legislative districts since 1901, though its population had shifted to cities. Urban voters said their votes were diluted, denying equal protection.
opts.reasoning: Justice Brennan listed the markers of a political question, starting with a textual commitment of the issue to another branch and "a lack of judicially discoverable and manageable standards." An equal protection claim against a state has neither: equal protection standards are familiar to courts.
opts.dissent: Justice Frankfurter, joined by Justice Harlan, warned that courts had no standard for judging how districts should be drawn and should leave apportionment to the political process.

blocks.html: Why have the doctrine at all? Some decisions are committed by the Constitution itself to Congress or the President, and some questions have no legal standard a court could apply; a judge would just be choosing a policy. Deciding such questions would make courts political actors and could weaken the respect their judgments need. On the other hand, labeling a claim "political" can leave a constitutional wrong without a judicial remedy, so the Court uses the doctrine sparingly.

blocks.html: Baker v. Carr (1962) held malapportionment claims justiciable and listed the markers of a political question. Nixon v. United States (1993): how the Senate "tries" impeachments is committed to the Senate. Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), 5 to 4: partisan gerrymandering claims are beyond federal courts for lack of manageable standards.

blocks.title: Textual commitment: Nixon v. United States (1993)
blocks.q: Federal judge Walter Nixon, convicted of perjury, was impeached. The Senate had a committee hear the evidence and report to the full Senate, which convicted him. He argued the Constitution requires the whole Senate to "try" him. Can courts review that?
steps: Article I, Section 3 gives the Senate "the sole Power to try all Impeachments."
The word "sole" commits the matter to the Senate alone, and "try" is too broad to supply a precise judicial standard.
Judicial review would also undercut the impeachment check on the judiciary itself.
blocks.a: No. The Court held the claim nonjusticiable; how to conduct the trial is for the Senate.

blocks.title: No manageable standard: Rucho v. Common Cause (2019)
blocks.q: Voters challenged congressional maps drawn to favor one party (Republicans in North Carolina, Democrats in Maryland). Can federal courts decide how much partisanship is too much?
steps: Chief Justice Roberts for the majority: the Constitution supplies no standard for "fair" partisan shares; courts would be making political judgments.
He noted other routes: state constitutions and courts, independent commissions and Congress under the Elections Clause.
Justice Kagan, for four dissenters, argued that lower courts had developed workable tests and that the harm to voters is serious.
blocks.a: The claims are political questions beyond the reach of federal courts (5 to 4).

blocks.html: Thinking Baker v. Carr refused to decide the case. It held the claim justiciable, opening the door to "one person, one vote" (Reynolds v. Sims, 1964). Its list of factors is used to explain when courts should decline, as in Nixon and Rucho. Check: did the Court reach the merits (or send the case back to do so)? Then it was justiciable.
The doctrine echoes Federalist No. 78's picture of courts with "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment": they act through legal judgment, and where there is no law to apply, they step back.

blocks.html: You read Article I in Civics and Government and saw federalism in Federalism Basics. Constitutional law starts every question about Congress with one premise: the national government has only the powers the Constitution grants. Article I begins, "All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress." The states, by contrast, have a general police power: the power to make laws for health, safety, morals and welfare without pointing to a list.

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: Article I, Section 8 lists most of Congress's powers: taxing and spending (clause 1), borrowing, commerce (clause 3), naturalization, coinage, post offices, patents, war, armies and navies, and the Necessary and Proper Clause (clause 18).

blocks.html: Why a list? The framers wanted a national government strong enough to do what the Articles of Confederation could not, such as tax, regulate trade among the states and raise an army, but no stronger. A list does both jobs: it grants real powers and, by naming them, implies that others were not granted. Madison put it this way in Federalist No. 45: "The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government, are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State governments are numerous and indefinite." The Tenth Amendment (1791) confirms the design: powers not delegated "are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people."

Congress has only enumerated powers: mainly those in Article I, Section 8, plus the enforcement clauses of later amendments (the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, Fifteenth and others). There is no general federal police power. Every federal law must trace to a granted power.

blocks.title: Tracing a law to a power
blocks.q: Congress passes a law setting safety standards for trucks that cross state lines. Which power supports it?
steps: Ask: what does the law regulate? Vehicles moving in interstate commerce.
Find the grant: Article I, Section 8, Clause 3, "To regulate Commerce … among the several States."
If the law needs supporting rules (inspections, records), the Necessary and Proper Clause covers those means.
blocks.a: The Commerce Clause, with the Necessary and Proper Clause for the means.

blocks.title: No police power
blocks.q: Could Congress pass a general law setting the age at which anyone in the country may marry, with no link to commerce, taxing, spending or any other granted power?
steps: Look for an enumerated power. Marriage age, by itself, is not on the list.
States regulate marriage under their police power.
Without a hook to a granted power, a federal law would have no constitutional basis.
blocks.a: No, not as a freestanding regulation. Congress would need a granted power, for example attaching conditions to federal grants under the spending power, which has its own limits (Conditions on Federal Money).

blocks.html: Reading the General Welfare Clause as a power to do anything for the general welfare. Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 is a power "To lay and collect Taxes … to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare." It is a power to tax and spend for those purposes, not a general power to regulate. Madison answered this very misreading in Federalist No. 41, calling it a "misconstruction." Check: does the law spend money, or does it command people? Commands need another power.

The ratification debate turned on this list. Anti-Federalists such as Brutus argued that the taxing power, read with the General Welfare and Necessary and Proper Clauses, had no real limit; the Federal Farmer feared a consolidated government. Federalists answered with Federalist No. 45 and Federalist No. 33. See both sides on the ratification debate page. The next lesson shows how the Supreme Court first read the list in McCulloch v. Maryland.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: Nothing in Article I mentions a bank or a corporation. Yet Congress chartered the First Bank of the United States in 1791, after a famous debate in which Hamilton argued it was constitutional and Jefferson and Madison argued it was not. Congress chartered the Second Bank in 1816. In 1818 Maryland taxed every bank in the state not chartered by Maryland, a tax aimed at the Baltimore branch of the national bank. Its cashier, James McCulloch, refused to pay. The case put the enumerated powers to their first great test.

opts.facts: Maryland sued James McCulloch, cashier of the Baltimore branch of the Second Bank of the United States, for issuing notes without paying the state's tax on banks not chartered by Maryland.
opts.reasoning: (1) The bank: the Constitution grants great powers (to tax, borrow, regulate commerce, wage war) and the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose reasonable means to carry them out. "Necessary" means convenient or useful, not "absolutely necessary." (2) The tax: the Constitution and federal laws are supreme; "the power to tax involves the power to destroy," so a state may not tax a federal institution.

blocks.html: Marshall used several modalities. Text: where the framers wanted strict necessity they said "absolutely necessary" (Article I, Section 10, on state import duties); in the Necessary and Proper Clause they did not. The clause is also placed among Congress's powers, not its limits. Structure: a constitution must mark only "great outlines," and "we must never forget that it is a Constitution we are expounding." History: the First Congress had chartered a bank after full debate. Supremacy: a part cannot control the whole, and Maryland's voters elect no one in Congress, so their tax would burden the people of every other state.

doc.title: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819): the test for means
paras: Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the Constitution, and all means which are appropriate, which are plainly adapted to that end, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the Constitution, are Constitutional.

marks.text: Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the Constitution
marks.note: The END must come from an enumerated power. The clause does not add new ends.
The MEANS must be appropriate to the end: a real connection, not absolute necessity.
The means may not violate another part of the Constitution, such as the Bill of Rights.

blocks.cap: Tap each phrase: the end, the fit, and the limits.

blocks.html: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), unanimous: Congress may charter a national bank as a means "plainly adapted" to its enumerated ends under the Necessary and Proper Clause; a state may not tax the bank, because "the power to tax involves the power to destroy."

blocks.title: Applying the McCulloch test
blocks.q: Congress, using its power to establish post offices and post roads, makes it a federal crime to steal mail. Nothing in Article I mentions crimes about mail. Is the law valid?
steps: End: running a postal system is an enumerated power (Article I, Section 8, Clause 7). Legitimate.
Means: protecting mail from theft is plainly adapted to running the post.
Not prohibited: no other clause forbids it.
blocks.a: Yes. This is the kind of implied means McCulloch approves.

blocks.title: Where McCulloch stops
blocks.q: A senator says, "Under McCulloch, Congress may pass any law that is useful to the country." What is wrong with that?
steps: McCulloch's first condition is that the END be legitimate, within the scope of the Constitution.

Marshall also warned that if Congress, "under the pretext of executing its powers," pursued objects "not intrusted to the Government," the Court would have to say the act "was not the law of the land."
Usefulness to the country is not an enumerated end.
blocks.a: McCulloch is about means. The end must still come from a granted power.

blocks.html: Thinking McCulloch says Congress can do whatever is useful. The clause gives broad choice of means to carry out enumerated ends. Check: name the enumerated power first, then ask whether the law is a reasonable means to it.

Marshall's reading tracks Madison's argument in Federalist No. 44: "wherever the end is required, the means are authorized." Hamilton made a similar point about the "sweeping clause" in Federalist No. 33. Brutus had feared exactly this reading, arguing that "necessary and proper" would let Congress do almost anything. The debate continues in Necessary and Proper Today.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: McCulloch gave Congress wide choice of means. Two modern cases show how the test works today and where justices draw the edge. Both accept McCulloch; they ask whether a particular measure is a reasonable means that respects a government of limited powers.

opts.facts: A federal law let the government keep in civil commitment, after their prison terms ended, federal prisoners found to be sexually dangerous because of a mental illness, until a state would take responsibility for them.
opts.reasoning: Justice Breyer pointed to five considerations together: the breadth of the clause; Congress's long history of federal involvement in prisons and mental health care for prisoners; sound reasons for the law, as the custodian of its prisoners; the law's accommodation of state interests; and its narrow scope.
opts.dissent: Justice Thomas, joined in part by Justice Scalia, argued that the law carried out no enumerated power: civil commitment of dangerous persons is a state police power.

blocks.html: Why ask whether a law is "proper" as well as "necessary"? The clause uses both words. "Necessary" asks about fit: is the law a reasonable means to an enumerated end? "Proper," on the reading in NFIB, asks whether the means respects the Constitution's structure: a means that would give Congress a power the Constitution withheld, or that would remove the limits on another power, is not proper even if it is useful.

opts.facts: The Affordable Care Act (2010) required most people to obtain health insurance or make a payment to the IRS (the "individual mandate"). The government defended it under the Commerce Clause and the Necessary and Proper Clause, and also as a tax.
opts.reasoning: On the Necessary and Proper Clause, Chief Justice Roberts wrote that even if the mandate was necessary to the Act's insurance reforms, it was not a "proper" means, because it would let Congress create the very commerce it then regulates by compelling people to buy a product. The mandate was upheld under the taxing power instead (see The Taxing Power).

blocks.html: United States v. Comstock (2010), 7 to 2: civil commitment of dangerous federal prisoners is a rational means connected to enumerated powers. NFIB v. Sebelius (2012): Chief Justice Roberts wrote that the individual mandate was not a "proper" means under the clause. Both apply McCulloch; they differ on whether a measure respects limited powers.

blocks.title: Comstock's chain of means
blocks.q: Where is the enumerated power in Comstock? Nothing in Article I mentions prisons.
steps: Congress has enumerated powers (commerce, taxing, and others) and may make federal crimes as means of carrying them out.
Prisons are a means of enforcing those crimes; care and custody of prisoners is a means of running prisons.
Commitment of a dangerous prisoner at release is, in the majority's view, a reasonable means of responsible custody.
The dissent answered that each step makes the link to an enumerated power weaker, and that the last step reaches a state concern.
blocks.a: The majority accepted a chain of means rooted in enumerated powers; the dissent thought the chain had become too long. Notice the disagreement is about application, not about McCulloch.

blocks.title: Comparing the two
blocks.q: Why did the Necessary and Proper Clause support the law in Comstock but not the mandate in NFIB, according to the controlling opinions?
steps: Comstock: the law managed people already in federal custody, a role the national government already held.
NFIB: the mandate would have drawn people who were not engaged in commerce into a market so that Congress could regulate them, a power the Commerce Clause itself did not give.
Roberts saw that as using the clause to create a new substantive power, not to carry out an existing one.
blocks.a: Comstock carried out an existing federal role; the mandate, in Roberts's view, would have expanded the commerce power itself.

blocks.html: Treating Comstock and NFIB as contradictory. Both accept McCulloch's test for means; they reach different results on different measures. Check: what enumerated power is the law carrying out, and does the means respect the structure of limited powers?

Madison expected the clause to be read as a grant of means only, in Federalist No. 44; Brutus warned it would be read to grant power over nearly everything. The two modern cases show both concerns at work.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: The Commerce Clause gives Congress power "To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes." Under the Articles of Confederation, states taxed and blocked one another's trade, and Congress could do nothing about it; that was a main reason for the Convention (you saw it in The Commerce Power). The first great case on the clause came in 1824, five years after McCulloch, and it was about steamboats.

opts.facts: New York gave Robert Fulton and Robert Livingston a monopoly on steamboats in New York waters; Aaron Ogden held a license from them. Thomas Gibbons ran competing steamboats between New Jersey and New York under a federal coasting license issued under a 1793 act of Congress. Ogden won an injunction in New York's courts.
opts.reasoning: Marshall defined each word. "Commerce" is more than buying and selling: "Commerce, undoubtedly, is traffic, but it is something more: it is intercourse," and it includes navigation. "Among" means "intermingled with," so the power does not stop at a state's border. To "regulate" is "to prescribe the rule by which commerce is to be governed." The federal license, a valid regulation of commerce, overrode the conflicting state monopoly under the Supremacy Clause.

blocks.html: Marshall read the clause broadly because the problem it solved was national. A power that stopped at each state line would leave Congress unable to govern a voyage from one state into another, exactly the kind of trade the states had been fighting over. But he also drew a line: the clause does not reach "that commerce which is completely internal, which is carried on between man and man in a State, or between different parts of the same State, and which does not extend to or affect other States." It reaches "that commerce which concerns more States than one."

Gibbons v. Ogden (1824): "commerce" includes navigation and all commercial intercourse; "among the several States" reaches commerce that concerns more states than one, even inside a state's borders; a valid federal law overrides a conflicting state grant. Purely internal commerce of a state remains with the state.

doc.title: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824): defining the words
paras: Commerce, undoubtedly, is traffic, but it is something more: it is intercourse.

The word "among" means intermingled with. A thing which is among others is intermingled with them. Commerce among the States cannot stop at the external boundary line of each State, but may be introduced into the interior.
Comprehensive as the word "among" is, it may very properly be restricted to that commerce which concerns more States than one.

marks.note: Commerce includes navigation and the movement of people and goods, not only sales.
So federal power can follow interstate commerce inside a state.
The limit: commerce wholly within one state, not affecting others, is left to that state.

blocks.cap: Tap each phrase.

blocks.title: Applying Gibbons's line
blocks.q: Under Gibbons alone, which of these could Congress regulate? (a) A ferry carrying passengers between two states. (b) A shop selling bread to neighbors in one town, with no effect elsewhere. (c) A riverboat running from one city in a state to another, carrying cargo bound for a third state.
steps: (a) Navigation between states: commerce that concerns more states than one. Yes.
(b) Completely internal commerce that does not affect other states. Not under Gibbons's line.
(c) The voyage is inside one state, but the cargo is part of interstate trade. "Intermingled" commerce: yes.
blocks.a: (a) and (c). Later cases would move the line, as the rest of this unit shows.

blocks.title: Where the limits come from
blocks.q: Marshall wrote that the restraints on Congress's commerce power lie in "the wisdom and the discretion of Congress, their identity with the people, and the influence which their constituents possess at elections." What kind of check is that?
steps: Not a judicial limit on how much Congress may regulate within the clause.
A political check: voters can remove members who regulate unwisely.
This idea returns in Garcia (1985), which left states' protection mostly to the political process.
blocks.a: A political safeguard. Gibbons defined the clause's scope; within it, the check is elections.

blocks.html: Thinking Gibbons let Congress regulate everything. It defined "commerce" broadly and let federal power reach inside state borders, but it expressly left "completely internal" commerce to the states. Check: does the activity concern more states than one?
Madison explained the need for the clause in Federalist No. 42, and Hamilton described the trade wars among the states under the Articles in Federalist No. 22. Next: the Court's narrow era.

blocks.html: After the Civil War, railroads and huge corporations built a national economy. Congress responded with the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) and the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890). From about 1887 to 1936 the Court read the commerce power through a set of categories that let much of that economy escape federal reach, while upholding other laws. Read the era as doctrine, not just as a list of struck-down laws.

head: Case
Law
Result and reasoning
rows: United States v. E. C. Knight Co. (1895), 8 to 1
Sherman Act applied to a sugar-refining trust controlling about 98 percent of U.S. refining
Not reached. Manufacturing is not commerce; its effect on commerce was only "indirect." Justice Harlan dissented.
Champion v. Ames (1903)
Federal ban on carrying lottery tickets across state lines
Upheld. Congress may prohibit the interstate movement of things it judges harmful.
Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918), 5 to 4
Ban on interstate shipment of goods made with child labor (Keating-Owen Act, 1916)
Struck down. The goods were harmless; the law really regulated manufacturing, a state matter. Justice Holmes dissented.
Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935), 9 to 0
National Industrial Recovery Act codes applied to a Brooklyn poultry business
Struck down. Local business with only indirect effects; also an unlawful delegation (see Nondelegation).
Carter v. Carter Coal Co. (1936)
Wage and hour rules for coal mining
Struck down. Mining is production, not commerce; effects on commerce were indirect.

blocks.html: The categories had a logic. If "commerce" meant everything that eventually affects trade, the commerce power would swallow the states' police power, and the enumerated-powers design would collapse. So the Court separated production (manufacturing, mining, agriculture) from commerce (buying, selling, transporting), and direct effects on commerce from indirect ones. Critics then and now answered that the lines were unworkable in an integrated economy: a sugar trust controls the price of sugar sold in every state.

From 1887 to 1936 the Court separated manufacturing from commerce (E. C. Knight, 1895), struck down the federal child-labor shipping ban (Hammer v. Dagenhart, 1918) and New Deal codes and coal rules (Schechter, 1935; Carter Coal, 1936) using a direct-indirect effects test, while upholding many laws on goods moving across state lines (Champion v. Ames, 1903).

blocks.title: Champion and Hammer side by side
blocks.q: Both laws barred goods from interstate shipment. Why did the Court uphold one and strike the other?
steps: Champion: lottery tickets were themselves seen as harmful, so stopping their movement regulated commerce.
Hammer: the goods made by children were harmless; the majority said the real aim was to regulate working conditions in factories, a matter for the states.
Justice Holmes, dissenting in Hammer, said the power to regulate interstate commerce includes the power to prohibit it, whatever Congress's motive.
blocks.a: The majority looked at the law's purpose and the nature of the goods. Darby (1941) later adopted Holmes's view and overruled Hammer.

blocks.title: Direct or indirect?
blocks.q: Under the narrow-era test, how would the Court treat a federal law setting wages for workers in a local factory whose products are sold in other states?
steps: The workers are engaged in production, not commerce (E. C. Knight, Carter Coal).
Wages affect interstate commerce only indirectly, through prices and output.
So the law would likely fall, as in Carter Coal.
blocks.a: Struck down under the narrow-era doctrine. The same law would be upheld after 1937.

blocks.html: Thinking the Court struck down every economic law of the era. It upheld railroad rate regulation, the lottery ban in Champion v. Ames and many laws on goods moving across state lines. The losing laws regulated production or local business. Check: was the law aimed at things moving in commerce (often upheld) or at production (often struck)?

Historians and scholars still debate the era. Some see judges protecting liberty of contract and their own economic views; others see a sincere effort to keep the enumerated-powers line that the framers drew. You will meet the due process side of the era in Constitutional Law II.

blocks.html: By early 1937 the Court had struck down major New Deal laws in the narrow era. On February 5, 1937, President Franklin D. Roosevelt proposed a bill letting him appoint an additional justice for each sitting justice over 70 who did not retire, up to six. Within weeks the Court changed course. Whether the plan caused the change is one of the most argued questions in American legal history.

opts.facts: The National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act, 1935) protected workers' right to organize. The NLRB ordered Jones & Laughlin, one of the largest steel companies, to rehire workers fired for union activity. The company said manufacturing was beyond the commerce power.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Hughes wrote that the test is the effect on interstate commerce, not whether the activity is "production." A strike at a huge, integrated steel company drawing materials from many states and shipping across the country would have a serious, even catastrophic, effect on interstate commerce. Congress may protect commerce from such burdens.

blocks.html: The new approach rests on a practical point: in a national economy, production and commerce are linked. If Congress may protect interstate commerce, it must be able to reach activities whose disruption would burden that commerce, even if they take place inside one plant. The question became one of degree: a close and substantial relation to interstate commerce. That logic carried the Court to Darby and then to Wickard.

opts.facts: The Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) set minimum wages and maximum hours for workers producing goods for interstate commerce and barred shipping goods made in violation.
opts.reasoning: Justice Stone, for a unanimous Court: Congress may exclude goods from interstate commerce for any reason not forbidden by the Constitution, and may regulate production that affects commerce. Hammer v. Dagenhart was overruled. The Tenth Amendment "states but a truism that all is retained which has not been surrendered": it adds no separate limit.

blocks.html: NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel (1937), 5 to 4, upheld the Wagner Act's reach to a steel company whose labor disputes would substantially affect interstate commerce. United States v. Darby (1941), unanimous, upheld federal wage and hour rules and overruled Hammer v. Dagenhart.

blocks.title: Did the court plan cause the switch?
blocks.q: Lay out the evidence on each side.
steps: For a link: the turn came within weeks of the plan; Justice Owen Roberts, who had joined narrow-era majorities, joined the new ones; the phrase "the switch in time that saved nine" was coined then.

Against a simple link: West Coast Hotel (decided March 29, 1937) was argued in December 1936, before the plan was announced; doctrine had been shifting in some earlier cases; and the plan failed in the Senate in July 1937.
Lasting change also came from appointments: Roosevelt named several justices from 1937 on, beginning with Hugo Black after Justice Van Devanter retired.
blocks.a: Historians disagree. Most agree the plan, public opinion, the 1936 election and new appointments all played parts; how much each mattered is debated.

blocks.title: Overruling Hammer
blocks.q: How did Darby treat the argument that a ban on shipping goods was really aimed at regulating production?
steps: Hammer had looked behind the law to its purpose.
Darby said Congress's motive does not matter if the regulation is within the commerce power.
It adopted Holmes's Hammer dissent: the power to regulate commerce includes the power to prohibit it.
blocks.a: Motive no longer decides the question. Hammer was "overruled."

blocks.html: Crediting the change entirely to the court-packing plan. Jones & Laughlin was decided while the plan was pending, and historians debate how much it mattered; West Coast Hotel was argued before the plan; new appointments soon reshaped the Court. Check the dates before drawing a cause-and-effect conclusion.
The 1937 turn is also the start of deferential review of economic laws, the subject of Rational Basis Review.

blocks.html: After 1937, the Court asked whether an activity substantially affects interstate commerce. Wickard v. Filburn (1942) added the idea that made the modern commerce power so broad: aggregation. A single farmer's wheat may not matter to the national market, but the Court looks at the total effect of everyone doing the same thing.

opts.facts: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 set wheat quotas to raise prices. Roscoe Filburn, an Ohio farmer, was allotted 11.1 acres but planted 23 and harvested 239 bushels over his quota. He kept the extra wheat on his farm for seed, feed for his animals and his family's flour. He was fined about 117 dollars.
opts.reasoning: Justice Jackson wrote that even if an activity is local and not itself commerce, Congress may reach it if it exerts a substantial economic effect on interstate commerce. Wheat grown for home use supplies a need that would otherwise be met by buying wheat, so it affects demand and price. Filburn's share was trivial by itself, but "taken together with that of many others similarly situated" it was far from trivial.

blocks.html: Why aggregate? Congress regulates whole markets, not single farms. A quota system aimed at national supply and price would fail if every farmer could grow unlimited wheat "for home use," because home-grown wheat replaces wheat that would have been bought. The question is whether the class of activity substantially affects commerce. If it does, Congress may regulate each instance in the class, even a small one.
Wickard v. Filburn (1942): Congress may limit wheat grown for use on a farmer's own farm, because the aggregate effect of many farmers doing the same would substantially affect interstate commerce.

blocks.title: Following Filburn's wheat
blocks.q: Trace the economic chain the Court relied on.
steps: Filburn grows extra wheat and feeds it to his chickens.
So he does not buy that much wheat on the market.
Multiply by many farmers: national demand for wheat falls.
Lower demand pushes down the price that Congress's quota system was designed to raise.
blocks.a: Home-grown wheat affects the national market through demand. That is a substantial effect in the aggregate.

blocks.title: Testing the limits of aggregation
blocks.q: Could the same reasoning reach any activity at all, if you add up enough instances? How did later cases answer?
steps: Wickard aggregated an economic activity: producing a commodity sold in a national market.
In Lopez (1995) and Morrison (2000) the Court refused to aggregate noneconomic activity (gun possession, violent crime).
In Raich (2005) it applied Wickard to another commodity grown at home.
blocks.a: Aggregation applies to economic activity. That limit was set decades after Wickard.

blocks.html: Thinking Filburn sold his extra wheat across state lines. He did not sell it at all; he used it on his farm. The aggregation principle, not any sale, brought it within the commerce power. Check: is the court adding up the effect of the whole class of activity?

Supporters of Wickard say it recognizes how markets work and that Congress, accountable to voters, is the right body to regulate them. Critics, including some justices, say it removes nearly every limit on the commerce power and departs from the clause's original meaning. Justice Thomas has written separately to urge reconsidering the substantial-effects test (as in his Lopez concurrence).

blocks.html: Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to end segregation in public life. Title II forbade discrimination based on race, color, religion or national origin in hotels, restaurants, theaters and other "public accommodations" whose operations affect commerce. Which power supported it? Most people would guess the Fourteenth Amendment. Congress relied mainly on the Commerce Clause, and the Court upheld it on that ground.

opts.facts: The Heart of Atlanta Motel had 216 rooms, sat near interstate highways, advertised in national media and drew about 75 percent of its guests from out of state. It refused to rent rooms to Black guests and challenged Title II.
opts.reasoning: Justice Clark, for a unanimous Court: Congress had heard extensive evidence that discrimination by hotels and motels discouraged Black Americans from traveling between states, burdening interstate commerce. Congress may regulate local activities that affect commerce, and its motive (a moral wrong) does not defeat the regulation.

opts.facts: Ollie's Barbecue, a family restaurant in Birmingham, Alabama, served few interstate travelers but bought much of its meat from a supplier who obtained it from out of state. It refused to seat Black customers in its dining room.
opts.reasoning: Applying Wickard's aggregation, the Court held that discrimination by restaurants, taken together, reduced spending and the flow of goods across state lines. Congress had a rational basis for finding a substantial effect.

blocks.html: Why the Commerce Clause and not the Fourteenth Amendment? The Fourteenth Amendment says "No State shall…"; it limits governments. In the Civil Rights Cases (1883) the Court had struck down the Civil Rights Act of 1875, which banned discrimination in inns, theaters and transport, holding that Congress's Fourteenth Amendment power did not reach private businesses. Rather than ask the Court to overrule that decision, Congress grounded Title II mainly in the commerce power, which reaches private conduct affecting commerce.

Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States and Katzenbach v. McClung (both 1964, unanimous) upheld Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 as a regulation of interstate commerce: through interstate travelers (the motel) and food shipped across state lines (the restaurant).

blocks.title: Two routes to the same result
blocks.q: Explain the different commerce links in the two 1964 cases.
steps: Heart of Atlanta: the motel served interstate travelers directly; discrimination burdened interstate travel.
McClung: the restaurant served mostly local customers, but bought food that had moved across state lines; discrimination by many such restaurants reduced that flow (aggregation).
Both rested on findings Congress made in hearings.
blocks.a: Travel for the motel, goods and aggregation for the restaurant.

blocks.title: Motive and the commerce power
blocks.q: The motel argued that Congress's real aim was moral, not commercial. What did the Court say?
steps: Under Darby (1941), Congress's motive does not matter if the law regulates commerce.
That Congress also saw discrimination as a moral wrong did not make the law invalid.
The Court also rejected arguments that the law took property without due process or imposed involuntary servitude.
blocks.a: A valid commerce regulation stands whatever moral purpose it also serves.

blocks.html: Thinking the 1964 Act's public accommodations rules rested on the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court upheld them under the Commerce Clause, partly because the Civil Rights Cases (1883) had limited Congress's Fourteenth Amendment power over private businesses. Check: does the law regulate private businesses? Then ask which power reaches private conduct.

Justices Douglas and Goldberg wrote concurrences saying the Fourteenth Amendment could also support the law. The limits of Congress's Fourteenth Amendment power return in Enforcing the Civil War Amendments and United States v. Morrison.

blocks.html: For 58 years after 1937, the Court did not strike down a federal law as beyond the commerce power. Many observers thought the clause had no judicial limits left. In 1995 that changed. Wickard and the civil rights cases were still good law; the question was whether there was anything the commerce power could not reach.

opts.facts: Alfonso Lopez, a 12th-grade student in San Antonio, Texas, brought a handgun to school. He was charged under the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990, which made it a crime to possess a firearm in a school zone. The Act had no requirement that the gun have any connection to interstate commerce.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist set out three categories of commerce regulation and found the Act fit none. Possessing a gun near a school is not economic activity, the law had no "jurisdictional element" tying each case to commerce, and the government's chain of effects (guns, violence, education, productivity, the economy) would leave no limit on federal power. The Constitution withholds a general police power from Congress.
opts.dissent: Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg, argued that Congress could rationally find that gun violence near schools harms education and so the national economy.

blocks.html: Why draw a line here? If the government's argument prevailed, Congress could regulate any activity, from family law to education, by pointing to some chain of effects on the economy. That would erase the difference between enumerated powers and the states' general police power, which the Constitution assumes. The Court chose economic activity as the category that can be aggregated, because that keeps Wickard and the civil rights cases while marking an outer edge.

blocks.html: United States v. Lopez (1995), 5 to 4: the Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeded the commerce power. Congress may regulate (1) the channels of interstate commerce, (2) its instrumentalities and persons or things in it, and (3) activities that substantially affect it. Possessing a gun near a school is not economic activity.

blocks.title: Sorting into the categories
blocks.q: Which Lopez category supports each law? (a) A ban on transporting kidnapped people across state lines. (b) Rules on airplane maintenance. (c) Rules on hotel discrimination against interstate travelers.
steps: (a) Keeps the channels of commerce free of harmful uses: category 1.
(b) Protects an instrumentality of commerce (airplanes): category 2.
(c) Regulates an activity that substantially affects interstate travel (Heart of Atlanta): category 3.

blocks.title: Why the Act failed category 3
blocks.q: List the features the majority relied on.
steps: The activity, possession of a gun, is not commercial or economic.
The Act had no jurisdictional element requiring a link to commerce in each case.
Congress made no findings on the effect on commerce (not required, but helpful).
The link to commerce depended on "piling inference upon inference," which would justify regulating anything.
blocks.a: Noneconomic activity, no jurisdictional hook and an attenuated chain of effects.

blocks.html: Mixing up the three Lopez categories. Channels are the routes (highways, waterways); instrumentalities are the vehicles and things moving on them; the third category is activities with substantial effects. Check: is the law about the road, about what travels on it, or about an activity elsewhere that affects it?

Justice Kennedy, joined by Justice O'Connor, concurred to stress the states' role in education and the stability of earlier precedent. Justice Thomas concurred to urge a return to the clause's original meaning, trade and transportation. Read the framers' Federalist No. 45 on "few and defined" federal powers alongside the opinion.
