blocks.html: Five years after Lopez, the Court faced a law with something the Gun-Free School Zones Act lacked: extensive congressional findings. The question was whether findings could save a law aimed at noneconomic activity.

opts.facts: The Violence Against Women Act of 1994 included a civil remedy: a person harmed by a crime of violence motivated by gender could sue the attacker in federal court. A college student sued two fellow students under that provision.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist: gender-motivated violence is not economic activity, and its effects on commerce could not be aggregated as in Wickard. Congress's findings relied on the same chain of effects rejected in Lopez; findings do not by themselves make a law valid. On Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment: the Amendment limits states, and the civil remedy targeted private individuals, not state action (following the Civil Rights Cases of 1883).
opts.dissent: Justice Souter, joined by three others, argued that Congress's mountain of findings showed a substantial effect on the economy and deserved deference.

blocks.html: The opinion protects the line Lopez drew. If findings about cumulative economic effects were enough, Congress could reach any crime, since every crime has economic costs. The Court said the regulation and punishment of violent crime not directed at commerce is the clearest example of the police power the Constitution leaves to the states. The Section 5 holding follows from the Fourteenth Amendment's text: "No State shall…"

United States v. Morrison (2000), 5 to 4: the Violence Against Women Act's civil remedy exceeded the commerce power (gender-motivated violence is not economic activity, and it cannot be aggregated) and Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment (which does not reach private conduct).

blocks.title: Two powers, two answers
blocks.q: The government defended the civil remedy under two powers. Walk through each.
steps: Commerce Clause: the activity (violent crime) is noneconomic; under Lopez it cannot be aggregated; findings do not change that.

Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment: Congress may enforce the Amendment against states. The remedy was aimed at private attackers, not states, so it was not "appropriate legislation" under Section 5 (see Enforcing the Civil War Amendments).
blocks.a: Neither power supported the provision.

blocks.title: Findings and the Court
blocks.q: Why did congressional findings not save the law?
steps: The majority said that whether an activity substantially affects commerce is finally a question for the courts, not for Congress.
The findings followed a "but-for" chain from crime to the national economy, the same reasoning Lopez rejected.
The dissent answered that courts should defer to Congress's factual judgment, as they did in the 1960s.
blocks.a: The findings described the same attenuated chain. Deference to findings is a key point of disagreement between majority and dissent.

blocks.html: Thinking Morrison struck down the whole Violence Against Women Act. Only the civil-remedy provision was at issue. The rest of the Act, including funding programs, remained in force, and Congress has reauthorized it several times. Check: which provision was challenged?

blocks.html: After Lopez and Morrison, some thought the Court was cutting back the commerce power broadly. Gonzales v. Raich (2005) showed where the limits stopped. The case involved a conflict between federal and state law on medical marijuana.

opts.facts: California's Compassionate Use Act (1996) allowed patients to grow and use marijuana for medical purposes on a doctor's recommendation. Angel Raich and Diane Monson grew marijuana at home for their own medical use. Federal agents seized and destroyed Monson's plants under the Controlled Substances Act (1970), which bans manufacturing and possessing marijuana.
opts.reasoning: Justice Stevens: the case is Wickard again. Marijuana is a commodity with an established interstate market (illegal, but a market). Congress could rationally conclude that home-grown marijuana, in the aggregate, would affect supply and demand in that market and undercut its comprehensive regulatory scheme. Unlike Lopez and Morrison, the activity, producing a commodity, is economic.
opts.dissent: Justice O'Connor, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and in part by Justice Thomas, said the case was closer to Lopez and that states should be free to experiment. Justice Thomas also wrote that the clause could not reach a plant grown and consumed in one state that never entered any market.

blocks.html: The majority's logic is the same as Wickard's. Production of a commodity, even for home use, is economic activity, because it replaces purchases on the market. And when Congress regulates an entire market, the Necessary and Proper Clause lets it reach local pieces that would otherwise leave a gap in the scheme. Justice Scalia, who concurred in the judgment, emphasized that second point.

Gonzales v. Raich (2005), 6 to 3: Congress may apply the Controlled Substances Act to marijuana grown at home for medical use under state law, because producing a commodity is economic activity that, in the aggregate, affects a national market Congress regulates comprehensively.

blocks.title: Distinguishing Lopez
blocks.q: The plaintiffs argued their activity was local and noncommercial, like Lopez's gun. How did the majority distinguish Lopez?
steps: Lopez involved possession of a gun, not economic activity, and a single-subject criminal statute.
Raich involved producing a commodity, which is economic activity.
It also involved a comprehensive scheme regulating a whole national market, which local exceptions would undercut.
blocks.a: Economic activity within a comprehensive scheme. Lopez was distinguished, not overruled.

blocks.title: What Raich did not decide
blocks.q: Did Raich hold that California's law was invalid or that states must punish medical marijuana?
steps: No. The case decided only whether federal law could be applied to the plaintiffs.
States remain free to set their own criminal laws; federal and state law can differ.
Whether to change federal law is a question for Congress.
blocks.a: Raich decided the reach of federal power, not the validity of the state law or the wisdom of either policy.

blocks.html: Thinking Raich overruled Lopez. The Court distinguished Lopez: Raich involved economic activity (producing a commodity) within a comprehensive regulatory scheme. Check: is the activity economic, and is it part of a market Congress regulates as a whole?

Notice the unusual line-up: Justice Scalia, often an advocate of limits on federal power, joined the result, and justices who often favor federal power formed the majority alongside him. The case shows that commerce clause votes do not always follow the patterns people expect.

blocks.html: The Affordable Care Act (2010) required most Americans to have health insurance or make a "shared responsibility payment" to the IRS. Twenty-six states and a business group challenged this "individual mandate." The government's main defense was the commerce power, with the Necessary and Proper Clause in support. The case brought every thread of this unit together.

opts.facts: The mandate required people not otherwise covered to buy insurance or pay. The government argued that everyone eventually uses health care, so the uninsured shift costs to others, and the mandate was needed to make the Act's insurance reforms work.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts, and four dissenting justices in a joint opinion, concluded that the Commerce Clause lets Congress regulate existing commercial activity, but not compel people to become active in commerce by buying a product. Being uninsured is not activity. Five justices agreed on that point. Roberts then held the payment valid as a tax (see The Taxing Power), so the mandate was upheld, 5 to 4.
opts.dissent: Justice Ginsburg, joined by three justices on this point, would have upheld the mandate under the commerce power: the health care market is one everyone enters, and Congress may regulate how people pay for care they will use.

blocks.html: The majority's concern was a power with no stopping point. If Congress could order people to buy insurance because their failure to buy affects commerce, it could order them to buy almost anything: vegetables to improve health, cars to help an industry. Every precedent in this unit had involved people already engaged in some activity. Ginsburg answered that health care is unique, since nearly everyone will need it and hospitals must treat emergencies, so the uninsured are already in the market.

In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), five justices concluded that the Commerce Clause did not support the individual mandate, because it compelled people to enter commerce rather than regulating existing activity. The mandate was nonetheless upheld as a tax, 5 to 4.

The Necessary and Proper Clause could not supply the missing power, Roberts said, because the mandate was not a "proper" means.

blocks.html: Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 gives Congress power "To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States." It was one of the main reasons for the Constitution: under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could only ask the states for money. In NFIB you saw a law fail under the commerce power and survive as a tax. This lesson explains how courts decide what counts as a tax.

Every tax changes behavior: a tax on tobacco discourages smoking, a tax on imports favors goods made at home. So the Court has long held that a tax is valid even if it also discourages the thing taxed, as long as it raises revenue and is not really a punishment for breaking a rule Congress could not otherwise make. Otherwise, the taxing power could become a back door around the limits on the other powers, a fear Brutus pressed in 1787 and that Hamilton answered in Federalist No. 33 and Federalist No. 36.

opts.facts: After Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918) struck down the child-labor shipping ban, Congress passed the Child Labor Tax Law (1919): employers who knowingly used child labor owed a tax of 10 percent of their annual net profits, however few children or however briefly.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Taft wrote that this was a penalty to regulate, not a tax: the heavy, fixed exaction applied only to employers who departed from a detailed code of conduct, applied only if they did so knowingly (a "scienter" requirement, typical of punishment), and let the Secretary of Labor, not just tax officers, inspect factories at any time. Upholding it would let Congress regulate anything by labeling a penalty a tax.

blocks.html: Congress may tax to raise revenue even if the tax also discourages conduct. A so-called tax that functions as a penalty for violating a regulation Congress could not otherwise impose may fail (Bailey v. Drexel Furniture, 1922). Courts look at function, not label.

blocks.title: NFIB: a "penalty" that is a tax
blocks.q: The Affordable Care Act called its payment a "penalty." Why did Chief Justice Roberts treat it as a tax for constitutional purposes?
steps: The label does not control: courts look at how the exaction works.
The payment was not so high that people had no real choice; for most it was less than the cost of insurance.
It had no scienter requirement, was collected by the IRS through ordinary means and could not lead to criminal prosecution.
It would raise revenue (about 4 billion dollars a year was projected).
blocks.a: It functioned as a tax, so it was within the taxing power, upheld 5 to 4. The four joint dissenters argued Congress had chosen the word "penalty" and meant it.

blocks.title: Applying the factors
blocks.q: Congress imposes a "fee" of 50,000 dollars, collected by the Justice Department, on anyone who knowingly fails to file a certain report, with no connection to income. Tax or penalty?
steps: Size: a large fixed amount, likely leaving no real choice.
Scienter: only knowing violations, a mark of punishment.
Collection: by a law enforcement agency, not the IRS.
Purpose: to stop the conduct, not to raise revenue.
blocks.a: Under Bailey and NFIB, it looks like a penalty. Whether it is valid would then depend on whether some other power supports the underlying rule.

blocks.html: Thinking the label Congress uses decides whether something is a tax. Courts look at function: NFIB treated a "penalty" as a tax, and Bailey treated a "tax" as a penalty. Check: size, scienter, who collects, and whether it raises revenue.

There is a separate question, beyond this course, of whether a tax is a "direct" tax that must be apportioned among the states by population (Article I, Section 9). NFIB held the mandate payment was not a direct tax. The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) removed apportionment for income taxes.

blocks.html: The same clause that lets Congress tax lets it spend: taxes are laid "to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare." But what does "general Welfare" limit? Madison and Hamilton, coauthors of the Federalist, gave different answers, and the Supreme Court did not choose between them until 1936.

head: View
Who held it
What "general Welfare" means for spending
rows: Narrow (Madisonian)
James Madison
Spending must carry out one of Congress's other enumerated powers; "general Welfare" summarizes them and adds nothing.
Broad (Hamiltonian)
Alexander Hamilton (Report on Manufactures, 1791); Joseph Story
Congress may spend on any purpose that serves the general welfare, even if it could not regulate that subject directly.
blocks.cap: Two founders, two readings.

opts.facts: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 taxed food processors and used the money to pay farmers to reduce their crops, aiming to raise farm prices.
opts.reasoning: Justice Owen Roberts adopted Hamilton's view: the spending power "is not limited by the direct grants of legislative power." But the Court struck down the program anyway, holding that it was a scheme to regulate agricultural production, a matter reserved to the states by the Tenth Amendment, and that the payments were coercive contracts.
opts.dissent: Justice Stone, joined by Justices Brandeis and Cardozo, argued that the power to spend includes the power to set conditions on the money, and that courts should not judge the wisdom of spending.

blocks.html: Why would Butler adopt the broad view and still strike down the law? The two holdings answer different questions. The first asks what Congress may spend money on: any general-welfare purpose. The second asked whether Congress could use spending to regulate what it could not regulate directly. Within a year that second holding faded: the Court upheld the Social Security Act in 1937, and later cases treated Butler's Tenth Amendment reasoning as abandoned while keeping its Hamiltonian reading.

Congress may spend for the general welfare, a power not limited to the subjects of its other enumerated powers (United States v. Butler, 1936, adopting Hamilton's view over Madison's). Helvering v. Davis (1937) upheld Social Security's old-age benefits.

opts.facts: The Social Security Act of 1935 taxed employers and employees and paid old-age benefits from the Treasury.
opts.reasoning: Justice Cardozo: Congress, not the courts, decides what serves the general welfare, unless its choice is clearly wrong. The problem of old age without income had become national in scope, and states acting alone could not solve it, since a state with generous benefits would attract the needy and drive away taxpayers.

blocks.title: Butler's two holdings
blocks.q: A classmate says, "Butler upheld the farm program because it adopted the broad view of spending." Correct it.
steps: Holding 1: the spending power is not limited to the other enumerated powers (Hamilton's view). Good for Congress.
Holding 2: the AAA used taxing and spending to regulate farm production, invading powers reserved to the states. Bad for this law.
Result: the AAA was struck down, 6 to 3.
blocks.a: Butler accepted the broad view of spending but struck down the Act.

blocks.title: Who decides what is "general welfare"?
blocks.q: Congress funds a national program to fight a disease. A taxpayer argues it serves only some regions. How would a court applying Helvering respond?
steps: Helvering says the line between general and particular welfare is for Congress to draw, not the courts, unless the choice is clearly arbitrary.
A disease program can serve the nation even if some places benefit more.
The taxpayer would probably also lack standing to sue.
blocks.a: Courts defer heavily to Congress's judgment of the general welfare.

blocks.html: Thinking Butler upheld the farm program it reviewed. Butler accepted the broad, Hamiltonian view of spending but struck down the Agricultural Adjustment Act on Tenth Amendment grounds. Check which question each holding answers: what may Congress spend on, and may it use spending to regulate?

Madison's narrow reading is in Federalist No. 41, where he calls the claim that the words grant an unlimited power a "misconstruction." Note that Madison was answering a claim about a power to regulate; whether Congress may spend beyond the other powers is the question Butler took up. The same year as Helvering, Steward Machine Co. v. Davis (1937) upheld the Act's unemployment insurance tax and credit. See the debate on the ratification debate page.

blocks.html: Congress cannot order a state to set a drinking age. But it can give states highway money. Can it give the money only to states that set the drinking age at 21? Most federal grants to states come with conditions, so this question, the limits on conditional spending, governs a large share of American government. It builds on the spending power.

opts.facts: The National Minimum Drinking Age Act of 1984 told the Secretary of Transportation to withhold 5 percent of certain federal highway funds from any state that allowed people under 21 to buy alcohol. South Dakota, which let 19-year-olds buy some beer, sued.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist set out the limits on conditions and found each met. The condition served the general welfare; it was stated unambiguously; it related to the federal interest in safe interstate highways, since young drivers crossed state lines to drink; it required nothing unconstitutional of the state; and losing 5 percent of highway funds was "relatively mild encouragement," not compulsion.
opts.dissent: Justice O'Connor argued the condition was not reasonably related to highway spending; it regulated who may drink. Justice Brennan also dissented.

head: Dole's limits on conditions
In plain words
rows: 1. General welfare
The spending must serve the general welfare (courts defer to Congress).
2. Unambiguous
States must know the condition when they accept the money.
3. Related (germane)
The condition must relate to the federal interest in the program.
4. No independent bar
The condition cannot require the state to do something unconstitutional.
5. Not coercive
The pressure cannot turn into compulsion.
blocks.cap: The test from South Dakota v. Dole (1987).

blocks.html: Why may Congress attach conditions at all? A grant is like a contract: the state may take the money with its terms or refuse it. That preserves state choice, which is what separates conditional spending from commands (see Anti-Commandeering). The limits exist because the choice must be real. If the condition is hidden, unrelated or so large a threat that no state could refuse, the "contract" becomes a command.

opts.facts: The Affordable Care Act expanded Medicaid to more low-income adults and told states that if they did not expand, they could lose all of their existing federal Medicaid funds, not just the new money.
opts.reasoning: Seven justices held this coercive. Chief Justice Roberts wrote that Medicaid funds made up over 10 percent of a state's overall budget; threatening all of them to force acceptance of a new program was "a gun to the head," not encouragement. The remedy: Congress could offer the new money with conditions but could not take away existing Medicaid funds from states that declined the expansion.

blocks.html: South Dakota v. Dole (1987), 7 to 2, upheld withholding 5 percent of highway funds from states with a drinking age under 21. Conditions must serve the general welfare, be unambiguous, relate to the program, not require unconstitutional acts and not be coercive. NFIB (2012) held the threat to all existing Medicaid funds coercive.

blocks.title: Applying Dole to a new condition
blocks.q: Congress offers states school-lunch money on condition that they adopt a particular rule for state income taxes. Walk through Dole.
steps: General welfare: school lunches serve it. Fine.
Unambiguous: suppose the statute states the condition clearly. Fine.
Relatedness: a state income tax rule has little to do with school lunches. This is the weak point.
Coercion: depends on the size of the threatened funds.
blocks.a: The condition is vulnerable on relatedness, the factor Justice O'Connor said Dole applied too loosely.

blocks.title: Dole versus NFIB on coercion
blocks.q: Why was 5 percent of highway funds acceptable but the Medicaid threat coercive?
steps: Dole: under 1 percent of South Dakota's budget was at stake, the Court noted; the state could realistically refuse.
NFIB: all existing Medicaid funds, over 10 percent of a state's budget, were at stake.
NFIB also stressed that the threat was used to force acceptance of a new, independent program, not to set terms on the existing one.
blocks.a: Size of the threat relative to the budget, and whether the threat reaches funds for a separate, existing program.

blocks.html: Thinking Congress can attach any condition to any money. Dole's limits apply, and NFIB found coercion when the threatened loss was a large share of a state's budget. Check all five limits, especially relatedness and coercion.

Justices Ginsburg and Sotomayor dissented on coercion in NFIB, arguing that Congress may always change the terms of its own program and that states kept a formal choice. The Court has not given a precise line for how much is too much.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: You have seen two ways Congress can influence states: it can pass federal laws that preempt state law, and it can offer money with conditions. There is a third thing it may not do: give orders to state governments, telling their legislatures what laws to pass or their officers what federal duties to perform. This is the anti-commandeering rule.

opts.facts: Congress, working with the states, set up a plan for disposing of low-level radioactive waste. The 1985 amendments offered money and access incentives, and added a "take title" provision: a state that did not provide for disposal of its waste by a deadline had to take ownership of it and become liable for it.
opts.reasoning: Justice O'Connor upheld the money and access incentives as valid uses of the spending and commerce powers, but struck down the take-title provision. It gave states a "choice" between two things Congress could not order on its own: taking title, or regulating as Congress directed. Congress may regulate people directly; it may not commandeer state legislatures to regulate for it.

blocks.html: Why the rule? The anti-commandeering cases give two main reasons. Accountability: if Congress orders states to carry out a federal program, voters may blame state officials for a choice Congress made, and the lines of responsibility blur. Structure: the Constitution created a government that acts directly on individuals, not one that governs through the states, as the Articles of Confederation had tried to do. States keep their own sovereignty and cannot be made agents of the federal government against their will.

opts.facts: The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act of 1993 required local chief law enforcement officers to run background checks on handgun buyers until a national instant system was ready. Sheriffs Jay Printz (Montana) and Richard Mack (Arizona) challenged the requirement.
opts.reasoning: Justice Scalia drew on history (early Congresses did not press state executives into service), structure and precedent to hold that Congress may not command state officers to administer a federal program.
opts.dissent: Justice Stevens, for four dissenters, pointed to early laws using state officials and argued that requiring state officers to help with a national problem is permissible.

blocks.html: Congress may not compel state legislatures to enact or enforce federal programs (New York v. United States, 1992) or order state officers to carry them out (Printz v. United States, 1997), and may not forbid states to repeal or change their own laws (Murphy v. NCAA, 2018).

opts.facts: The Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act (1992) made it unlawful for a state "to authorize" sports gambling. New Jersey repealed its own ban on sports betting at casinos and racetracks.
opts.reasoning: Justice Alito: telling a state legislature it may not repeal a law is as much a command as telling it to pass one. There is no distinction between ordering a state to do something and ordering it not to. The law did not preempt anything, because it did not regulate private actors.

blocks.title: Commandeering, preemption or spending?
blocks.q: Classify each. (a) Federal law sets emission standards for factories and displaces state standards. (b) Federal law orders state legislatures to adopt the federal emission standards. (c) Congress offers states money if they adopt the standards.
steps: (a) Regulates private factories directly and displaces state law: preemption, valid if within a federal power.
(b) Orders state legislatures to legislate: commandeering, invalid under New York.
(c) Offers money with conditions: conditional spending, valid if it meets Dole's limits.
blocks.a: Only (b) violates the anti-commandeering rule.

blocks.title: Reading Murphy
blocks.q: Why couldn't Congress defend PASPA as preemption?
steps: Preemption works through federal laws that regulate private conduct and so displace conflicting state laws.
PASPA did not regulate gamblers or casinos; it told states what laws they could have.
A rule addressed only to state legislatures is a command to the states, not a preemption.
blocks.a: Congress could have banned sports gambling directly, preempting state law. It could not tell states to keep their own bans.

blocks.html: Confusing commandeering with preemption. Congress may preempt state law or offer money with conditions; it may not issue direct orders to state governments to regulate. Check: is the federal law addressed to private people (preemption) or to the state as a government (commandeering)?

Federalists argued that the new government would act on individuals directly, unlike the Confederation, which could only make "requisitions" on states; see Hamilton in Federalist No. 15 and Federalist No. 16. Hamilton also wrote in Federalist No. 27 that federal laws would be enforced partly through state officers, a passage the Printz majority and dissent read differently.

blocks.html: The Tenth Amendment says: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." In Darby (1941) the Court called it "but a truism." Anti-commandeering showed one structural limit on Congress. This lesson asks a different question: when Congress regulates everyone, private employers and states alike, may it apply that law to the states themselves?

blocks.name: cv-doc

marks.text: not delegated to the United States
marks.note: What is reserved depends on what was delegated: the scope of Congress's powers.

marks.text: reserved to the States respectively, or to the people
marks.note: The amendment confirms the enumerated-powers design; whether it adds a separate limit is the question this lesson traces.

blocks.cap: Tap the marked phrases.

opts.facts: Congress extended the federal minimum wage and maximum hours rules of the Fair Labor Standards Act (1974 amendments) to almost all employees of states and cities.
opts.reasoning: Justice Rehnquist, for five justices, held that Congress may not use the commerce power to displace the states' freedom to structure "integral operations in areas of traditional governmental functions," such as fire protection, police, sanitation and parks. Doing so would impair states' ability to function in the federal system.

opts.facts: The San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority, a public bus system, argued that under National League of Cities it was exempt from federal wage and hour rules.
opts.reasoning: Justice Blackmun, who had joined National League of Cities, now wrote for five justices that the "traditional governmental functions" test was unworkable: nine years of lower-court decisions had produced no principled line between "traditional" and other state functions, with similar city services sorted into different boxes. The states' protection lies mainly in the structure of the federal government itself, the political process, since states are represented in Congress.
opts.dissent: Justice Powell, joined by three others, and Justices Rehnquist and O'Connor in separate dissents, warned that the decision left the Tenth Amendment without judicial force; Rehnquist predicted that the principle of National League would one day again win a majority.

blocks.html: The core question is who enforces federalism. One view: the courts must, because Congress has every incentive to expand its own power. The Garcia view: the Constitution protects states mainly through structure, since senators and representatives are elected from the states and answer to them, and courts are poorly placed to decide which state functions are "traditional." Later cases took a middle path: they did not revive National League, but they protected states through other doctrines: anti-commandeering, sovereign immunity and clear-statement rules.

National League of Cities v. Usery (1976) barred federal wage rules for state employees in "traditional governmental functions"; Garcia v. San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority (1985) overruled it, leaving states' protection mostly to the political process. Laws that apply generally to states and private parties alike are usually valid.

blocks.title: Generally applicable law or command?
blocks.q: Congress requires all employers, public and private, to keep records of overtime hours. A state objects. How does this differ from Printz?
steps: The law regulates the state as an employer, the same way it regulates private employers. That is a generally applicable law (Garcia).
Printz involved ordering state officers to administer a federal program aimed at private parties.
Under current doctrine, the generally applicable law is valid if within the commerce power.
blocks.a: Valid under Garcia. Commandeering concerns orders to govern; general laws that happen to include states are different.

blocks.title: Reading the Tenth Amendment
blocks.q: A student says the Tenth Amendment lists the powers that belong to the states. What is wrong?
steps: The amendment lists nothing; it reserves whatever was "not delegated."
So to know what is reserved, you must first know the scope of the delegated powers.
That is why most Tenth Amendment cases are really about the reach of the commerce, taxing or spending powers.
blocks.a: The Tenth Amendment is a rule of construction about leftovers, not a list.

blocks.html: Thinking the Tenth Amendment by itself lists powers that belong to the states. It reserves powers not delegated; which powers those are depends on the scope of the grants to Congress. Check: start with the federal power; the Tenth Amendment question follows.

The "political safeguards" argument echoes Madison in Federalist No. 45 and Federalist No. 46, which argue that the states, closer to the people, would be well able to defend themselves within the political system. The Federal Farmer doubted it, fearing consolidation. See the ratification debate page.

blocks.html: Can you sue a state? The Eleventh Amendment's text is narrow, but the doctrine of state sovereign immunity is broad, and much of constitutional litigation against states runs through its exceptions. It began with a lawsuit four years after the Constitution took effect.

opts.facts: The executor of a South Carolina merchant sued Georgia in the Supreme Court for payment for goods supplied during the Revolution. Georgia refused to appear, claiming it could not be sued.
opts.reasoning: Four justices, writing one by one (seriatim), read Article III's grant of jurisdiction over controversies "between a State and Citizens of another State" literally: it covered suits against states. Justice Iredell dissented, arguing that states kept the common-law immunity of sovereigns.
opts.later: Reversed by the Eleventh Amendment, ratified in 1795.

blocks.name: cv-doc

doc.title: The Eleventh Amendment (1795)
paras: The Judicial power of the United States shall not be construed to extend to any suit in law or equity, commenced or prosecuted against one of the United States by Citizens of another State, or by Citizens or Subjects of any Foreign State.

marks.note: It speaks as a rule of interpretation, correcting how Chisholm read Article III.

marks.text: by Citizens of another State, or by Citizens or Subjects of any Foreign State
marks.note: The text names only out-of-state and foreign plaintiffs. Hans v. Louisiana (1890) extended immunity to a state's own citizens.

blocks.cap: Read the text closely: whom does it name?

blocks.html: Why read the amendment more broadly than its words? The Court's view, from Hans v. Louisiana (1890) on, is that the amendment did not create immunity; it restored an immunity the states had when they ratified the Constitution, which Chisholm wrongly overlooked. Hamilton had said so in Federalist No. 81: "It is inherent in the nature of sovereignty not to be amenable to the suit of an individual without its consent." On the other side, Brutus (essay XIII) had warned that Article III would let individuals sue states, and some justices and scholars argue that the amendment means only what it says.

head: Case
Holding
rows: Hans v. Louisiana (1890)
A state's own citizen may not sue it in federal court without its consent.
Ex parte Young (1908)
A suit for an injunction against a state officer to stop enforcing an unconstitutional law is allowed.
Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer (1976)
Congress may abrogate state immunity when it enforces the Fourteenth Amendment (Section 5).
Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida (1996), 5 to 4
Congress may not abrogate state immunity using its Article I powers (overruling Pennsylvania v. Union Gas, 1989).
Alden v. Maine (1999)
States are also immune from private suits under federal law in their own courts.
blocks.cap: The doctrine and its main exceptions.

blocks.html: Chisholm v. Georgia (1793) let a citizen of another state sue Georgia; the Eleventh Amendment (1795) reversed it. Hans (1890) barred suits by a state's own citizens; Seminole Tribe (1996): Congress cannot abrogate immunity under Article I; Ex parte Young (1908): suits against state officers for injunctions are allowed.

blocks.title: Can this suit go forward?
blocks.q: A worker sues State X in federal court for back pay under a federal wage law passed under the commerce power. Then she sues the state labor commissioner for an order requiring the state to follow the law from now on.
steps: Suit 1 is against the state itself, for money, under an Article I law: barred by sovereign immunity (Seminole Tribe; and Alden would bar it in state court too), unless the state consents.
Suit 2 is against an officer, for prospective relief (an injunction): allowed under Ex parte Young.
The United States itself could also sue the state; immunity protects states from private suits.
blocks.a: Suit 1 fails; suit 2 can proceed.

blocks.title: When Congress can abrogate
blocks.q: Congress passes a law under Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment letting people sue states for intentional race discrimination in employment. Is immunity abrogated?
steps: Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer: the Fourteenth Amendment was adopted after the Eleventh and limits states; Congress may abrogate immunity under Section 5.
The law must be valid Section 5 legislation (see Enforcing the Civil War Amendments) and must say clearly that it abrogates immunity.
Targeting intentional race discrimination fits Section 5 well.
blocks.a: Yes, if Congress says so clearly and the law is valid Section 5 legislation.

blocks.html: Reading the Eleventh Amendment literally, as covering only suits by citizens of other states. The Court treats it as confirming a broader immunity that also bars suits by a state's own citizens (Hans), though some justices and scholars disagree. Check: who is suing, whom (state or officer), for what (money or an injunction), and under which power Congress acted.

blocks.html: The Thirteenth (1865), Fourteenth (1868) and Fifteenth (1870) Amendments each end with a grant of power: "Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation." These enforcement clauses were a major shift in federalism, giving Congress power to act against the states to protect rights. The questions are how far "enforce" reaches, and who decides what the amendments mean.

blocks.name: cv-amend
blocks.cap: The three Civil War amendments, 1865–1870.

blocks.html: Two views of "enforce." On one view, Congress may define the rights the amendments protect, at least to expand them, since it is the body the amendments chose to enforce them; Katzenbach v. Morgan (1966) used broad language along these lines. On the other, Congress may only remedy or prevent violations of rights as the Court defines them, because if Congress could redefine the Fourteenth Amendment, it could change the Constitution by statute, which Marbury forbids. City of Boerne adopted the second view.

opts.facts: After the Court held in Employment Division v. Smith (1990) that neutral, generally applicable laws do not violate the Free Exercise Clause, Congress passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993), requiring governments to justify substantial burdens on religion under strict scrutiny. A church in Boerne, Texas, denied a building permit under a historic-preservation ordinance, sued under RFRA.
opts.reasoning: Justice Kennedy: Section 5 power is "remedial." Congress may enact laws that prevent or remedy constitutional violations, even reaching some constitutional conduct, but there must be "congruence and proportionality" between the injury to be prevented and the means adopted. RFRA, which applied strict scrutiny to every law in the country without a record of widespread unconstitutional conduct, was out of proportion and in effect redefined the right.
opts.later: RFRA still applies to the federal government, as in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby (2014).

blocks.html: Congress may enforce the Fourteenth Amendment by "appropriate legislation," but under City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) a Section 5 law must show congruence and proportionality between the injury and the remedy. Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the Voting Rights Act's coverage formula (Section 4(b)) as based on old data; Section 2 remains.

opts.facts: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 required covered jurisdictions to obtain federal approval ("preclearance," Section 5) before changing voting rules. Section 4(b) chose the covered places using voting data from the 1960s and early 1970s. Congress reauthorized the Act in 2006 for another 25 years without changing the formula.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts: the Act's preclearance was an extraordinary departure from equal state sovereignty, justified in 1965 by exceptional conditions, as South Carolina v. Katzenbach (1966) held. But conditions had changed dramatically, and Congress could not keep using decades-old data to decide which states were covered. Section 4(b) was unconstitutional; Congress could write a new formula.
opts.dissent: Justice Ginsburg, for four justices, argued that Congress's 2006 record of continuing discrimination justified the formula and that preclearance was what had made progress possible.

blocks.title: What Shelby County did and did not do
blocks.q: After Shelby County, which parts of the Voting Rights Act still operate?
steps: Section 4(b), the coverage formula, was struck down.
Section 5 preclearance was not itself held invalid, but with no formula it applies to no one unless Congress writes a new one.
Section 2, which bans voting practices that discriminate on account of race nationwide, remained in force.
blocks.a: Section 2 and the rest of the Act still operate; preclearance is dormant without a formula.

blocks.title: Who decides what the amendment means?
blocks.q: Congress passes a law under Section 5 that requires every state to meet a standard stricter than anything the Court has found the Fourteenth Amendment to require, with no record of state violations. What question would a court ask under Boerne?
steps: Boerne says Congress may remedy or prevent violations of the right as the Court defines it, not redefine the right.
The court compares the injury Congress identified with the remedy it chose.
A sweeping remedy with little record of violations looks like a new rule, not enforcement.
blocks.a: Whether the law is congruent and proportional to a record of constitutional violations; without one, the law likely fails, as RFRA did.

blocks.html: Thinking Shelby County struck down the whole Voting Rights Act. It struck the coverage formula of Section 4(b); Section 2's nationwide ban remains. In 2026 the Court narrowed how Section 2 applies to redistricting. Check which section a case addresses before stating its effect.
Also remember Morrison (2000): Section 5 reaches state action, not private conduct. For the history of the Reconstruction amendments, see U.S. History I.

blocks.html: The Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law "the supreme Law of the Land … any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding." When federal and state law collide, federal law wins. That is preemption. You saw the basics in Federal and State Law; here are the categories courts use.

blocks.name: cv-doc

marks.text: which shall be made in Pursuance thereof
marks.note: Only valid federal laws preempt. A federal law beyond Congress's enumerated powers preempts nothing.

marks.text: any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding
marks.note: Where they truly conflict, state law gives way.

blocks.cap: The Supremacy Clause, Article VI, Clause 2.

head: Kind
When it applies
Example
rows: Express preemption
The federal statute says so in words
"No State may impose labeling requirements different from these."
Field preemption
Federal regulation is so pervasive, or the federal interest so dominant, that Congress left no room for states
Alien registration (Arizona v. United States, 2012)
Conflict: impossibility
It is impossible to comply with both federal and state law
Federal law requires a label; state law forbids it.
Conflict: obstacle
State law stands as an obstacle to the full purposes of federal law
A state penalty scheme that upsets a balance Congress chose
blocks.cap: Express and implied preemption.

blocks.html: Why a presumption against preemption? States are separate sovereigns with police power over health, safety and welfare. Courts assume Congress does not lightly displace that power, so in fields the states have traditionally occupied, they look for a clear and manifest congressional purpose before finding preemption (Rice v. Santa Fe Elevator Corp., 1947). The presumption respects both federal supremacy and the states' role. Some justices question the presumption in express-preemption cases, where the text should control.

Valid federal law preempts state law expressly (by its terms) or impliedly, when it occupies a field or conflicts with state law (compliance with both is impossible, or state law obstructs federal purposes). Courts apply a presumption against preempting traditional state powers.

blocks.title: Arizona v. United States (2012)
blocks.q: Arizona's S.B. 1070 added state crimes and powers concerning immigration. The United States challenged four provisions. How did the Court sort them?
steps: Section 3 (a state crime for failing to carry federal registration papers): field preemption; Congress occupied the field of alien registration.
Section 5(C) (a state crime for unauthorized workers seeking work): obstacle to Congress's choice to penalize employers, not workers.
Section 6 (warrantless arrests for removability): obstacle to the federal system for deciding removal.
Section 2(B) (officers to check immigration status during lawful stops): not preempted on its face, before the state courts had applied it.
blocks.a: Three of four provisions preempted, 5 to 3 (Justice Kennedy for the Court; Justice Kagan did not take part).

blocks.title: Overlap without preemption
blocks.q: A federal law sets minimum safety standards for a product and says nothing about state law. A state sets stricter standards. Is the state law preempted?
steps: Express: the federal statute says nothing. No.
Field: minimum standards suggest Congress expected others to add to them. Likely no.
Impossibility: a maker can meet both by meeting the stricter state rule. No.
Obstacle: unless the federal purpose was a single national standard, no.
blocks.a: Probably not preempted. Overlap alone is not preemption.

blocks.html: Thinking any overlap between federal and state law means preemption. Many state laws coexist with federal ones; preemption needs express words, a field Congress occupied, or a real conflict. Check the four categories in order.

Preemption is how Congress normally overrides states, and it is lawful as long as the federal law regulates private conduct within an enumerated power. Compare anti-commandeering, which forbids Congress to give orders to state governments. Hamilton discussed federal supremacy in Federalist No. 33.

blocks.html: The Commerce Clause is written as a grant of power to Congress. But since Gibbons the Court has also read it as a silent limit on the states, even when Congress has not acted. This "negative" or dormant Commerce Clause stops states from building walls against one another's trade. You know from Preemption that Congress can override state law; the dormant clause asks what states may do when Congress is silent.

Why read a limit into a grant? The main reason is the history: under the Articles of Confederation, states taxed and blocked each other's goods, and the Constitution was meant to create a national common market. Hamilton described those trade wars in Federalist No. 22, and Madison in Federalist No. 42. A second reason is political: a state that discriminates against out-of-state businesses burdens people who cannot vote in that state, so its own political process will not correct the harm. The doctrine has critics, too: Justices Scalia and Thomas argued it has no basis in the text and that Congress, not courts, should police state trade barriers.

opts.facts: New Jersey banned most solid and liquid waste from other states from entering its landfills, while letting New Jersey's own waste in. It argued the law protected its environment and its limited landfill space.
opts.reasoning: The Court: whatever the state's purpose, it may not achieve it by discriminating against articles of commerce coming from outside the state unless there is some reason, apart from their origin, to treat them differently. Out-of-state garbage was no more harmful than New Jersey's own. A state may not isolate itself from a problem common to many by closing its borders.
opts.dissent: Two dissenting justices compared the law to quarantine laws that keep out harmful items.

blocks.html: A state law that discriminates against interstate commerce, favoring in-state interests over out-of-state ones, is virtually per se invalid unless the state shows a legitimate local purpose that cannot be served by nondiscriminatory means (City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey, 1978; upheld in the rare case Maine v. Taylor, 1986).

blocks.name: cv-scrutiny
blocks.cap: Discrimination against interstate commerce gets review much like strict scrutiny: a legitimate purpose and no nondiscriminatory alternative.

blocks.title: The rare law that survives: Maine v. Taylor (1986)
blocks.q: Maine banned importing live baitfish from other states. Why did this discriminatory law survive?
steps: The law discriminated on its face: in-state baitfish could be sold, imported ones could not.
Maine showed a legitimate purpose: out-of-state baitfish could carry parasites and nonnative species harmful to Maine's wild fish.
Maine also showed that no adequate test or inspection could screen the fish, so no nondiscriminatory alternative existed.
blocks.a: Upheld. The test is hard to pass, but not impossible when the state proves a real difference and no other means.

blocks.title: Discrimination in effect
blocks.q: A state requires all milk sold there to be pasteurized at plants within five miles of the city center. Every plant within that radius is in the state. The law does not mention other states. Is it discriminatory?
steps: On its face the law is neutral: it names no state.
In effect it excludes all out-of-state processors, the way an outright ban would.
The state could protect health by inspecting distant plants, a nondiscriminatory alternative.
blocks.a: Discriminatory in effect, and likely invalid. Courts look at purpose and effect, not only the words.

blocks.html: Looking for discrimination only in a law's words. Laws neutral on their face can discriminate in purpose or effect. On the other hand, remember that some justices reject the doctrine entirely as lacking a textual basis. Check: who bears the burden and who gains: in-state or out-of-state interests?

Congress can always change the result: because the clause is a grant of power to Congress, Congress may authorize states to do what the dormant clause would otherwise forbid. The next lesson covers laws that do not discriminate: Pike balancing.

blocks.html: Most state laws treat in-state and out-of-state businesses the same, but many still burden interstate commerce: truck-length limits, labeling rules, product standards. Discrimination gets a near-fatal test. For even-handed laws, the Court uses a gentler balancing test from a 1970 case about cantaloupes.

opts.facts: Arizona required cantaloupes grown in Arizona to be packed in Arizona in containers identifying them as Arizona produce. Bruce Church, Inc., grew high-quality cantaloupes in Arizona but packed them at its plant across the state line in California. Complying would have required building a costly new packing plant in Arizona.
opts.test: "Where the statute regulates even-handedly to effectuate a legitimate local public interest, and its effects on interstate commerce are only incidental, it will be upheld unless the burden imposed on such commerce is clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits."
opts.reasoning: Arizona's interest in protecting the reputation of its growers was legitimate but small as applied here; requiring a business to build a plant in the state is a heavy burden. The burden was clearly excessive.

blocks.html: Why balance at all? An even-handed law does not show the protectionist danger of discrimination: in-state businesses bear the same burden, so they have a reason to fight bad laws in the state legislature. Courts therefore defer, stepping in only when the burden on interstate commerce is clearly out of proportion to the local good. Critics, including Justices Scalia and Gorsuch, have argued that judges cannot weigh such different things (economic burdens against, for example, safety or moral interests) on any common scale.

A nondiscriminatory state law is upheld unless the burden on interstate commerce is "clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits" (Pike v. Bruce Church, 1970). In Kassel v. Consolidated Freightways (1981) the Court struck down Iowa's ban on 65-foot double-trailer trucks: the safety gain was slight and the burden on interstate trucking was heavy.

blocks.title: Kassel v. Consolidated Freightways (1981)
blocks.q: Iowa banned 65-foot double-trailer trucks on its highways, though most nearby states allowed them, and cited highway safety. Interstate truckers had to detour around Iowa, use smaller trucks or split their loads at the border. How did the Court respond?
steps: The length limit applied to all trucks on Iowa roads, so the Court weighed burden against benefit.
Local benefit: the evidence showed the longer trucks were about as safe as the shorter ones Iowa allowed, so the safety gain was slight.
Burden: heavy, because interstate trucking had to go around the state or change equipment.
The judgment was 6 to 3; the dissenters would have given more weight to the state's safety judgment.
blocks.a: Iowa's law was struck down. Courts respect safety laws, but a claimed safety benefit that the evidence does not support cannot outweigh a large burden on interstate commerce.

blocks.title: Running the Pike test
blocks.q: A state requires trucks on its highways to use a special mudflap that no other state requires and many forbid. The state cites modest safety benefits. Interstate trucks must stop at the border to change mudflaps. Apply Pike.
steps: Even-handed? Yes: in-state and out-of-state trucks need the same mudflap.
Local benefit: modest, as the state concedes.
Burden: severe for interstate trucking, which must stop and re-equip at the border.
Compare: the burden is clearly excessive relative to the benefit.
blocks.a: Likely invalid under Pike.

blocks.html: Applying Pike to discriminatory laws. Discriminatory laws face the near-per-se rule from City of Philadelphia; Pike is for even-handed laws. Check the first question first: does the law treat in-state and out-of-state interests differently?

blocks.html: The dormant Commerce Clause limits states when they regulate commerce. But states also act like businesses: they buy supplies, sell products and run facilities. When a state acts as a market participant rather than a regulator, it may prefer its own residents, just as a private company may choose its customers.

opts.facts: South Dakota built and ran its own cement plant. During a cement shortage it gave South Dakota buyers first claim on the plant's output, cutting off a Wyoming company that had bought from the plant for years.
opts.reasoning: The five-justice majority: the Commerce Clause limits states as regulators of markets, not as participants in them. Like any private seller, South Dakota could choose its customers. The plant was built with state money at state risk, and residents who paid for it could share its output first.
opts.dissent: The four dissenters argued that the state was hoarding a scarce resource in a way the Commerce Clause forbids.

blocks.html: Why the exception? The dormant Commerce Clause aims at protectionist regulation that distorts a national market. When a state spends its own money, it bears the cost of its choices, as any business does, and its taxpayers have a fair claim to the benefits of what they paid for. Treating states like private parties in the marketplace also respects their sovereignty over their own resources. The exception has limits, though, because a state could otherwise use its buying power to regulate whole industries.

When a state acts as a buyer or seller rather than a regulator, it may prefer its own residents (Reeves, Inc. v. Stake, 1980). The exception covers the state's own market dealings, not conditions it imposes on later private transactions (South-Central Timber v. Wunnicke, 1984). United Haulers (2007) also upheld laws favoring a public waste facility over private ones.

blocks.title: Downstream limits: South-Central Timber (1984)
blocks.q: Alaska sold timber from state lands on condition that buyers process it in Alaska before shipping it out of state. Is this market participation?
steps: Selling timber is market participation; Alaska may set the price and choose buyers.
But requiring processing in Alaska reaches the next market, timber processing, in which Alaska is not a participant.
A private seller could not control what buyers do after the sale in this way; this is regulation dressed as a contract.
blocks.a: Not protected. The condition regulated a downstream market and violated the dormant Commerce Clause.

blocks.title: Public versus private: United Haulers (2007)
blocks.q: Two New York counties required all local trash haulers to bring waste to a facility owned by a public authority. Haulers argued this discriminated against out-of-state processors. Why did the Court uphold it?
steps: The law favored a public facility doing a traditional government job, not local private businesses over out-of-state ones.
Treating every favor to a government entity as discrimination would let courts second-guess ordinary public services.
So the law was not "discriminatory" under the near-per-se rule; under Pike, its burdens did not clearly exceed its benefits.
blocks.a: Upheld. Favoring a public entity is treated differently from favoring local private businesses. Justice Thomas, concurring, argued the dormant Commerce Clause should be abandoned altogether.

blocks.html: Thinking a state can use its spending to regulate anything downstream. The exception covers the state's own market dealings, not conditions it imposes on later private transactions (South-Central Timber). Check: is the state acting in the market it is part of, or controlling a different one?

Note that the market participant exception applies only to the dormant Commerce Clause. Discrimination against out-of-state citizens may still be challenged under Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause, which has no market participant exception.

blocks.html: Article IV, Section 2 says: "The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States." You saw it among the rules of interstate relations in Civics and Government. It overlaps with the dormant Commerce Clause but works differently: it protects people who are citizens of other states, it has a clear textual basis, and it has no market participant exception.

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: Article IV, Section 2, Clause 1.

blocks.html: The clause came from the Articles of Confederation, which had a similar guarantee. Its purpose, the Court has said, is to help fuse independent states into one nation: a citizen of Ohio who goes to Kentucky to work or do business should not be treated as a foreigner there. In Federalist No. 80, Hamilton called it "the basis of the Union." The clause does not require states to give out-of-staters every benefit; it protects rights fundamental to national unity, such as earning a living.

head: Step
Question
rows: Does the law discriminate against citizens of other states (often by residency)?
Does it burden a "privilege" protected by the clause: one fundamental to national unity, such as pursuing a common calling or doing business?

If so, is there a substantial reason for the difference, and does the discrimination bear a substantial relationship to it (are nonresidents a peculiar source of the problem; are there less restrictive means)?
blocks.cap: The test from Toomer v. Witsell (1948) and later cases.

blocks.html: Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause bars states from discriminating against citizens of other states in fundamental matters such as earning a living, unless there is a substantial reason closely related to the discrimination (Toomer v. Witsell, 1948; Supreme Court of New Hampshire v. Piper, 1985).

blocks.title: Toomer v. Witsell (1948)
blocks.q: South Carolina charged 25 dollars for a shrimp-boat license to residents and 2,500 dollars to nonresidents. Apply the test.
steps: Step 1: the fee discriminates against nonresidents.
Step 2: commercial shrimping is a common calling, earning a living: a protected privilege.
Step 3: the state pointed to conservation and enforcement costs, but nothing showed nonresidents caused a special problem, and a hundredfold difference was not closely related to any extra cost.
blocks.a: Invalid. A state may charge nonresidents more to cover real extra costs, but not a fee that shuts them out.

blocks.title: Recreation versus livelihood: Baldwin (1978)
blocks.q: Montana charged nonresidents far more than residents for elk-hunting licenses. Does the clause apply?
steps: Step 1: yes, the fee discriminates against nonresidents.
Step 2: recreational big-game hunting is not fundamental to the nation as a single entity; it is not a way of earning a living.
So the clause does not apply, and the law stands.
blocks.a: Upheld, because the privilege at stake was not fundamental. Compare Piper (1985): practicing law is a common calling, so New Hampshire could not limit bar admission to residents.

blocks.html: Applying the clause to corporations. It protects citizens, which corporations are not for this purpose (Paul v. Virginia, 1869); corporations rely on the dormant Commerce Clause instead. Check: is the challenger an individual citizen of another state?

blocks.html: Article II begins: "The executive Power shall be vested in a President." You studied the President's formal powers in Civics and Government. Does the Vesting Clause grant powers beyond those listed, such as a general power to act in an emergency? The leading case arose in 1952, in the middle of the Korean War.

opts.facts: Facing a nationwide steel strike that he believed would cripple war production, President Truman issued Executive Order 10340 on April 8, 1952, directing Secretary of Commerce Charles Sawyer to take possession of most of the country's steel mills. No statute authorized the seizure; when Congress passed the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947 it had considered and declined to give the President seizure power for labor emergencies.
opts.reasoning: Justice Black, for the Court: the President's power must come from an act of Congress or the Constitution. No statute authorized this, and the order was not a military act of the Commander in Chief. It was lawmaking, which the Constitution gives to Congress.
opts.dissent: Chief Justice Vinson, joined by Justices Reed and Minton, argued that the President had to act to keep the war effort supplied and to carry out laws Congress had passed.

blocks.html: Justice Robert Jackson's concurrence became the most cited part of the case because it explains why the answer depends on Congress. "While the Constitution diffuses power the better to secure liberty, it also contemplates that practice will integrate the dispersed powers into a workable government." Presidential powers "are not fixed but fluctuate, depending upon their disjunction or conjunction with those of Congress." When the two political branches agree, the whole power of the federal government stands behind the action; when they conflict, the President has only what the Constitution gives him that Congress cannot take away.

head: Zone
Situation
Presidential power
rows: The President acts with express or implied authorization of Congress
"At its maximum, for it includes all that he possesses in his own right plus all that Congress can delegate"
Congress has neither granted nor denied authority
A "zone of twilight," where the President and Congress may share power; the outcome depends on the facts of the moment
The President acts against the express or implied will of Congress
"At its lowest ebb": only the President's own constitutional powers minus Congress's powers over the matter
blocks.cap: Justice Jackson's three zones (quotations from the concurrence).

blocks.html: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952), 6 to 3: President Truman lacked power to seize the steel mills. Justice Jackson's concurrence set out three zones: power is greatest with Congress's authorization, uncertain in a "zone of twilight" when Congress is silent, and "at its lowest ebb" against Congress's will.

blocks.name: cv-branches
blocks.cap: Youngstown is about the line between the legislative and executive boxes, and the courts' power to police it.

blocks.title: Placing the seizure in a zone
blocks.q: Which zone did Jackson place Truman's seizure in, and why?
steps: Congress had addressed labor emergencies in several statutes, and in the Taft-Hartley Act it had chosen not to give the President seizure power.
So the seizure was incompatible with the implied will of Congress: zone 3.
In zone 3 the President must rely on powers Congress cannot touch. Neither the Commander-in-Chief power nor the Vesting Clause reached seizing domestic industry.
blocks.a: Zone 3, the lowest ebb. The seizure failed.

blocks.title: Using the zones on new facts
blocks.q: A statute expressly authorizes the President to impose sanctions on foreign banks in a declared emergency. The President does so. A bank challenges the action. Where does the analysis start?
steps: Congress expressly authorized the action: zone 1.
The action is valid unless the federal government as a whole lacks the power, or it violates a right (such as due process).
Courts give the strongest presumption of validity in zone 1.
blocks.a: Zone 1: power at its maximum. The challenger must show the whole federal government lacks the power.

blocks.html: Quoting Jackson's concurrence as the majority opinion. Justice Black wrote for the Court with a stricter view: the President may act only under a statute or a specific constitutional power. Jackson's framework, though only a concurrence, became the most cited part of the case and is now used by the Court itself (for example in Zivotofsky v. Kerry and Medellín v. Texas). Check who wrote what before quoting.

Hamilton argued for "energy" in the executive in Federalist No. 70 and distinguished the President from a king in Federalist No. 69; Madison's Federalist No. 47 warned that combining legislative and executive power is "the very definition of tyranny." The Anti-Federalist Cato feared a President with too much power. Youngstown is where those arguments meet a real emergency.

blocks.html: Article I vests "All legislative Powers herein granted" in Congress. Modern government runs largely on statutes that leave the details to agencies, which you met in Administrative Law Basics. If only Congress may legislate, how much may it hand to others? The nondelegation doctrine answers that Congress may delegate the power to fill in details, but not its legislative power itself.

The doctrine rests on accountability and the structure of Article I. Lawmaking requires two houses and presentment, a process designed to be hard so that laws reflect broad agreement. If Congress could pass a statute saying "the agency shall make whatever rules it thinks best," it would escape both the process and the political responsibility for the choices. On the other hand, Congress cannot write every rule for a complex economy, and courts have found it hard to say how much discretion is too much.

Holding
rows: J. W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States (1928)
A delegation is valid if Congress lays down an "intelligible principle" to guide the delegate (tariff adjustments upheld).
Panama Refining Co. v. Ryan (1935)
Struck down: a provision of the National Industrial Recovery Act gave the President power over oil shipments with no standard.
Schechter Poultry (1935)
Struck down: NIRA codes of "fair competition" written largely by industry groups.

Upheld the Sentencing Commission, which writes federal sentencing guidelines; Justice Scalia dissented.

Upheld the Clean Air Act's command to set air standards "requisite to protect the public health" (Justice Scalia).

Upheld a delegation in a sex-offender registration law; Justice Gorsuch, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas, dissented and urged a stricter test.

blocks.html: Congress may delegate if it lays down an "intelligible principle" (J. W. Hampton, 1928). The Court has struck down delegations only twice, both in 1935. Courts also read statutes with care when an agency claims power over a question of vast "economic and political significance" (FDA v. Brown & Williamson, 2000): Congress is not presumed to hand over such decisions "in so cryptic a fashion." This line of cases is called the major questions doctrine.

opts.name: FDA v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp.
opts.q: Did the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act give the FDA power to regulate tobacco products?
opts.facts: In 1996 the Food and Drug Administration declared nicotine a "drug" and cigarettes and smokeless tobacco "devices" that deliver it, and issued rules limiting their sale and advertising, especially to young people. Tobacco companies sued, arguing the agency had no such authority.
opts.holding: No. Read as a whole, and alongside the tobacco laws Congress had passed over decades, the Act did not let the FDA regulate tobacco.
opts.reasoning: Justice O'Connor: the Act would have required the FDA to ban a product it found unsafe, yet Congress had repeatedly legislated on tobacco while keeping it on the market. Given tobacco's place in the economy, the Court was "confident that Congress could not have intended to delegate a decision of such economic and political significance to an agency in so cryptic a fashion."
opts.dissent: Justice Breyer, for four justices, argued that the Act's broad words covered nicotine and that the agency's reading fit the statute's purpose of protecting health.

blocks.title: Two ways to limit delegation
blocks.q: A statute tells an agency to regulate "devices" that affect the body. The agency announces that it will regulate an entire major industry that Congress has addressed in other laws for decades. A challenger brings two arguments. Name them.
steps: Nondelegation: the statute itself is unconstitutional because it gives away legislative power with no intelligible principle. This argument almost always fails.
Major questions: the statute is valid, but it should not be read to cover a decision of such economic and political significance without clear words from Congress, as in Brown & Williamson.
The first strikes down a law; the second reads a law narrowly.
blocks.a: The nondelegation argument attacks the statute; the major questions argument attacks the agency's reading of it.

blocks.title: Applying the intelligible principle test
blocks.q: A statute tells an agency to set workplace exposure limits for toxic substances "at the level that most adequately assures, to the extent feasible, that no employee will suffer material impairment of health." Is there an intelligible principle?
steps: The statute names the goal (protecting employee health) and the limit (feasibility).
Courts have upheld far vaguer standards ("public interest," "fair and equitable," "requisite to protect the public health").
Under current doctrine, this easily passes.
blocks.a: Yes. Whether the test should be stricter is the live debate, not the result here.

blocks.html: Thinking the nondelegation doctrine regularly strikes down laws. It has not been used to strike down a law since 1935, though several justices have called for reviving it (Gundy, 2019). Courts more often limit agency power by reading statutes narrowly. Check: did the Court strike the statute (nondelegation) or read it narrowly (major questions)?

Supporters of the major questions doctrine say it keeps the biggest policy choices with elected legislators; critics say it lets judges decide which questions are "major" and override the words Congress chose. Compare agency deference.

blocks.html: You traced how a bill becomes a law in Civics and Government. Article I, Section 7 makes that process a requirement: every bill must pass both houses (bicameralism) and be presented to the President to sign or veto (presentment). Two famous cases show what happens when Congress tries a shortcut.

blocks.name: cv-bill
blocks.cap: The only road to a federal law: both houses, then the President.

opts.facts: Immigration law let the Attorney General suspend the deportation of certain noncitizens, but either house of Congress could veto a suspension by resolution, without the other house or the President. The House vetoed the suspension of Jagdish Chadha's deportation.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Burger: the House's action changed Chadha's legal rights and so was legislative in character. Legislative action must follow the single, carefully designed procedure of Article I: passage by both houses and presentment. The one-house veto skipped both.
opts.dissent: Justice White argued that the legislative veto was a vital tool for Congress to keep delegated power in check, and noted that the decision cast doubt on a large number of statutes that contained one.

blocks.html: Why insist on the cumbersome process? The framers made lawmaking hard on purpose. Bicameralism forces agreement between two bodies elected differently; presentment lets the President, elected by the whole nation, check Congress. Each step protects liberty by making it harder to pass laws hastily or for narrow interests. If Congress could act with legal effect through one house alone, it would escape those checks.

opts.facts: The Line Item Veto Act of 1996 let the President, after signing a bill, "cancel" certain individual spending items and tax benefits in it. President Clinton canceled provisions benefiting New York City and a group of potato growers, who sued.
opts.reasoning: Justice Stevens: canceling part of a signed law repeals or amends it. The Presentment Clause lets the President approve or reject a bill as a whole, before it becomes law. There is no constitutional procedure for the President to amend or repeal parts of statutes. If Congress wants such a power, it must amend the Constitution.

blocks.html: INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down the one-house legislative veto: lawmaking requires passage by both houses and presentment to the President. Clinton v. City of New York (1998) struck down the Line Item Veto Act: canceling parts of signed laws amends them without Article I's process.

blocks.title: Is it "legislative"?
blocks.q: Which of these must go through bicameralism and presentment? (a) The House passes a resolution honoring a sports team. (b) The Senate confirms a cabinet nominee. (c) One house votes to overturn an agency rule, with legal effect.
steps: (a) A simple resolution with no legal effect on anyone's rights: no.
(b) The Constitution expressly gives the Senate alone the power to confirm: no (Chadha listed such exceptions).
(c) Changing legal rights and duties by one house alone: yes, so it is invalid as a one-house act.
blocks.a: Only (c). Congress can still overturn rules by passing a joint resolution through both houses and presenting it to the President, as the Congressional Review Act provides.

blocks.title: Clinton's cancellations and the veto
blocks.q: How is a line-item cancellation different from a regular veto?
steps: A veto happens before a bill becomes law; Congress can override it by two-thirds of each house.
A cancellation happened after the President signed the bill, changing a law already in force.
Changing a law requires a new law passed through Article I, Section 7.
blocks.a: A veto rejects a whole bill before enactment; a cancellation amends an enacted law, which only Congress can do through the full process.

blocks.html: Thinking the line-item veto was struck down as too much power for Congress. It was struck down because canceling parts of a law amounts to amending it without following Article I's process, giving the President a power the Constitution does not. Justice Kennedy's concurrence added that it also threatened liberty by concentrating power. Check which branch gained power and which procedure was skipped.

Related: in Bowsher v. Synar (1986), the Court held that Congress may not keep for itself the removal of an officer (the Comptroller General) who carries out the laws. Read Madison on the purposes of the two houses in Federalist No. 62 and Hamilton on the veto in Federalist No. 73.
