blocks.html: The Appointments Clause (Article II, Section 2, Clause 2) says the President "shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint" ambassadors, judges and "all other Officers of the United States," but "the Congress may by Law vest the Appointment of such inferior Officers, as they think proper, in the President alone, in the Courts of Law, or in the Heads of Departments." The President may also fill vacancies "during the Recess of the Senate." Three questions follow: who is an officer, who is inferior, and what is a recess?

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: The Appointments Clause.

blocks.html: The framers argued at length about who should appoint. Appointment by a legislature, common in the states, scattered responsibility; appointment by the executive alone risked favoritism. The compromise gave the President the choice, for accountability, and the Senate a check. Hamilton defended it in Federalist No. 76: one person chooses better, and the Senate's consent "would be an excellent check upon a spirit of favoritism." The clause also keeps Congress from appointing the officers who carry out its laws.

head: Question
Rule
Case
rows: Who is an "officer"?
Someone who holds a continuing position and exercises significant authority under federal law; ordinary employees are not officers.
Buckley v. Valeo (1976): Congress could not appoint members of the Federal Election Commission. Lucia v. SEC (2018): SEC administrative law judges are officers.
Who is "inferior"?
An officer whose work is directed and supervised by officers appointed by the President with Senate consent.
Edmond v. United States (1997); Morrison v. Olson (1988) looked at removability, limited duties, jurisdiction and tenure.
What is a "recess"?
A break long enough to count: a recess of fewer than ten days is presumptively too short.
NLRB v. Noel Canning (2014): appointments during a three-day break were invalid.
blocks.cap: The Appointments Clause in three questions.

blocks.html: Principal officers are appointed by the President with Senate consent; Congress may vest the appointment of inferior officers in the President, the courts or department heads (Edmond, 1997; Lucia v. SEC, 2018). Recess appointments need a recess of at least ten days, presumptively (NLRB v. Noel Canning, 2014).

opts.facts: In January 2012, during a period when the Senate held "pro forma" sessions every three days with no business conducted, the President appointed three members of the National Labor Relations Board as recess appointments. A company challenged an order of the Board.
opts.reasoning: Justice Breyer, for five justices: the clause covers both breaks between sessions and recesses within a session, but a break of fewer than ten days is presumptively too short. The Senate is in session when it says it is, provided it can conduct business. A three-day break did not count, so the appointments were invalid.
opts.dissent: Justice Scalia, for four justices, concurred in the judgment only, arguing that "the Recess" means only the break between sessions.

blocks.title: Officer or employee?
blocks.q: A federal agency hires (a) a clerk who files documents and (b) a hearing officer who presides over enforcement cases, takes testimony and issues decisions that become final unless reviewed. Which must be appointed under the clause?
steps: (a) The clerk exercises no significant authority under federal law: an employee.
(b) The hearing officer holds a continuing office and exercises significant discretion in enforcement cases, much like the SEC judges in Lucia.
So (b) is an officer; as an inferior officer, (b) may be appointed by the head of the department if Congress so provides.
blocks.a: Only (b) must be appointed under the Appointments Clause.

blocks.title: Principal or inferior?
blocks.q: Judges of a military appeals court were appointed by the Secretary of Transportation. Their decisions could be reviewed by another court, and a superior officer supervised their administration and could remove them. Were they inferior officers?
steps: Edmond asks whether their work is directed and supervised by Senate-confirmed officers.
Another executive body could review their decisions, and they could be removed from their assignments.
So they had a superior other than the President.
blocks.a: Inferior officers; appointment by the department head was valid (Edmond, 1997).

blocks.html: Thinking every executive employee is an "officer" needing Senate confirmation. Officers exercise significant authority under federal law; ordinary employees do not, and inferior officers may be appointed without the Senate if Congress so provides. Check: significant authority? Then who supervises?

blocks.html: The Constitution says how officers are appointed but says almost nothing about how they are removed, except by impeachment. Can the President fire any executive officer at will, or may Congress protect some officers by allowing removal only "for cause"? The answer shapes who controls federal agencies, and the Court's answer has moved over a century.

Officer
Holding

A postmaster
Congress may not require Senate consent for removal; the President may remove executive officers he appoints.

blocks.html: Two views compete. The unitary executive view: Article II vests "the executive Power" in one President and charges him to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed," so he must be able to remove those who exercise executive power for him; otherwise voters cannot hold anyone responsible. Its advocates point to the "Decision of 1789," when the First Congress debated and accepted presidential removal of department heads. The independent agency view: Congress, which creates offices, may decide some need insulation from politics, such as regulators of markets or elections; its advocates point to more than a century of independent commissions and to Hamilton's remark in Federalist No. 77 that the Senate's consent "would be necessary to displace as well as to appoint."

opts.facts: The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, led by a single director serving a five-year term and removable only for "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office." The director could write binding rules, bring enforcement suits and decide cases. Seila Law, a law firm, received a demand for documents and argued the agency's structure was unconstitutional.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts: the President's power to remove those who execute the laws is the general rule. The Court recognized only two exceptions: multi-member expert bodies (Humphrey's Executor) and inferior officers with limited duties (Morrison). A single director wielding significant executive power fit neither, and concentrated power in one person accountable to no one. The removal limit was cut from the statute; the agency itself could continue.
opts.dissent: Justice Kagan, for four justices, argued that the Constitution leaves the design of agencies to Congress and that for-cause limits had a long history.

blocks.html: Myers (1926) upheld the President's power to remove executive officers; Humphrey's Executor (1935) allowed limits for multi-member commissions; Morrison v. Olson (1988) upheld the independent counsel; and Seila Law (2020) struck down limits for a single director who wields significant executive power. The Court overruled Humphrey's Executor in 2026.

blocks.title: Applying Seila Law
blocks.q: Congress creates an agency led by one administrator who writes binding rules and brings enforcement suits, and allows removal only for cause. Is the removal limit valid under Seila Law?
steps: The administrator is a principal officer, not an inferior officer with limited duties, so Morrison does not help.
One person, not a multi-member body, heads the agency, and Seila Law refused to extend Humphrey's to that design.
The administrator wields significant executive power (rules, enforcement).
blocks.a: Invalid. Following Seila Law, a court would likely cut the removal limit and leave the agency in place.

blocks.title: Where Morrison fits
blocks.q: Is Morrison v. Olson still good law after Seila Law?
steps: Morrison upheld a for-cause limit on removing an inferior officer with limited duties and tenure.
Seila Law described Morrison as an exception for inferior officers with limited duties and no policymaking or administrative authority.
Seila Law did not overrule Morrison.
blocks.a: Morrison survives as a narrow exception for some inferior officers, though its reasoning has been criticized, most famously in Justice Scalia's dissent.

blocks.html: Thinking Humphrey's Executor protected every agency head. It covered only multi-member expert bodies, and the Court refused to extend it to single directors (Seila Law). Check: one head or a commission? A principal officer or an inferior one with limited duties?
For the history of the Decision of 1789 and the founding debate, see Federalist No. 76 and Federalist No. 77.

blocks.html: Foreign affairs powers are split between the branches. The President is Commander in Chief, makes treaties (with two-thirds of the Senate), appoints and receives ambassadors. Congress regulates foreign commerce, declares war, raises armies, funds everything and defines offenses against the law of nations. Youngstown's zones apply here too, but the Court has often given the President more room abroad than at home.

opts.facts: A 1934 joint resolution let the President ban arms sales to countries fighting in the Chaco War (Bolivia and Paraguay) if he found a ban would help restore peace. He did, and Curtiss-Wright was charged with selling machine guns to Bolivia. It argued the resolution delegated legislative power with no standard.
opts.reasoning: Justice Sutherland: delegations in foreign affairs are judged more leniently, because the federal government's external powers come from national sovereignty, not only from the enumeration, and because the President is "the sole organ of the federal government in the field of international relations."
opts.later: Its broad statements about inherent presidential power have been criticized by scholars and limited by later cases; the actual holding involved congressional authorization (zone 1).

blocks.html: Why give the President more room in foreign affairs? A single executive brings what Hamilton called "Decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch" (Federalist No. 70), and the nation must speak with one voice abroad. But the Constitution gives Congress major foreign powers, and the framers deliberately gave the war-declaring power to Congress. So the modern cases tend to ask whether Congress agreed, stayed silent or disagreed, and whether the Constitution gives the President a specific power that Congress cannot take away.

United States v. Curtiss-Wright (1936) described broad presidential power in foreign affairs; Dames & Moore v. Regan (1981) upheld executive agreements settling the Iran hostage claims; Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015) held the power to recognize foreign governments belongs to the President alone.

blocks.title: Dames & Moore v. Regan (1981)
blocks.q: To end the Iran hostage crisis in January 1981, the President agreed with Iran to end American lawsuits against Iran and send the claims to an international tribunal. A company with a claim challenged the agreement. How did the Court analyze it?
steps: For nullifying attachments of Iranian assets, a statute (IEEPA) gave the President authority: zone 1.

For suspending the claims themselves, no statute directly authorized it, but Congress had long accepted executive claims settlements and had not objected here: zone 2, with congressional acquiescence.
The Court stressed that its decision was narrow and tied to that history.
blocks.a: Upheld, using Youngstown's framework and long congressional acquiescence.

opts.facts: A 2002 statute directed the State Department, on request, to list "Israel" as the place of birth on passports of U.S. citizens born in Jerusalem. Presidents of both parties had long declined to recognize any nation's sovereignty over Jerusalem.
opts.reasoning: Justice Kennedy applied Youngstown's third zone. The text and structure of Article II (the power to receive ambassadors) and history show that the recognition power belongs to the President alone, and Congress may not command the President to contradict a recognition decision.

blocks.title: Recognition versus the rest
blocks.q: After Zivotofsky, can Congress refuse to fund an embassy in a country the President has recognized?
steps: Zivotofsky held only that the formal act of recognition is the President's alone.
The Court said Congress keeps broad powers over foreign affairs, including funding, trade and war.
Congress could decline funding; it could not make the President issue a formal statement contradicting recognition.
blocks.a: Probably yes. The recognition holding is narrow.

blocks.html: Thinking the President controls all foreign affairs. Congress regulates foreign commerce, declares war, funds the government and (through the Senate) approves treaties; Zivotofsky rested on the specific recognition power. Medellín v. Texas (2008) also held the President could not by himself make a non-self-executing treaty obligation binding on state courts. Check: is the President relying on a specific Article II power, or acting against Congress?

blocks.html: Congress has the power "To declare War"; the President is "Commander in Chief." You saw the war powers debate in Civics and Government. The courts rarely decide whether a war is lawful, but they have decided many cases about what the government may do to people during wartime. Read these cases for how much they depend on whether Congress authorized the action.

Question
Holding

Yes: the President may respond to an attack or rebellion without waiting for a declaration.
Ex parte Milligan (1866)

No.
Hamdi v. Rumsfeld (2004)
What process is due a U.S. citizen held as an enemy combatant?
Congress's 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force allowed detention, but the citizen must get notice and a fair chance to rebut before a neutral decisionmaker.

Were the Guantanamo military commissions lawful?
No: they were not authorized by Congress and violated the laws of war as Congress had adopted them.

Yes: the Suspension Clause reaches Guantanamo, and Congress had not provided an adequate substitute.

blocks.html: Why focus on Congress? Under Youngstown, presidential power is strongest with Congress's support. In Hamdi, the AUMF supplied authorization to detain. In Hamdan, the commissions failed because Congress had not authorized them in the form the President chose. After Hamdan, Congress passed the Military Commissions Act of 2006, and the next question, in Boumediene, was whether Congress could remove habeas corpus. So the cases were mostly a conversation among the three branches, not a free hand for one.

The Prize Cases (1863) upheld Lincoln's blockade before Congress acted. After 2001: Hamdi (2004) required due process for a citizen held as an enemy combatant; Hamdan (2006) held the military commissions unauthorized; Boumediene (2008) extended habeas corpus to Guantanamo.

opts.facts: Yaser Hamdi, a U.S. citizen, was captured in Afghanistan in 2001 and held in military prisons in the United States as an "enemy combatant," without charges or a hearing.
opts.reasoning: Justice O'Connor's plurality: the AUMF authorized detaining enemy combatants for the duration of the conflict, but due process requires that a citizen receive notice of the factual basis and a fair opportunity to rebut it before a neutral decisionmaker. She wrote that a state of war "is not a blank check for the President when it comes to the rights of the Nation's citizens."
opts.dissent: Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Stevens, argued that a citizen must be charged with a crime or Congress must suspend habeas corpus. Justice Thomas argued the detention was within the President's war powers.

blocks.title: Following the branches in the Guantanamo cases
blocks.q: Trace the back-and-forth from 2004 to 2008.
steps: 2004: Hamdi requires due process for citizens; Rasul v. Bush (same day) reads the habeas statute to reach Guantanamo.
2005–2006: Congress passes laws limiting detainee habeas cases; Hamdan holds the commissions unauthorized.
2006: Congress passes the Military Commissions Act, authorizing commissions and removing habeas jurisdiction.
2008: Boumediene holds the Constitution's habeas privilege applies, so Congress must provide an adequate substitute or suspend the writ.
blocks.a: Each decision prompted a response by Congress, and each statute shaped the next case.

blocks.title: The War Powers Resolution
blocks.q: Congress passed the War Powers Resolution in 1973, over President Nixon's veto. What does it require, and is it settled law?
steps: The President must report to Congress within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities and must end their use within 60 days (plus up to 30 days for withdrawal) unless Congress authorizes it.
Presidents of both parties have said it unconstitutionally limits the Commander-in-Chief power, while generally filing the reports.
The courts have not resolved the dispute, often treating such suits as nonjusticiable.
blocks.a: It is a statute both branches cite and contest; its constitutionality has never been decided by the Supreme Court.

blocks.html: Thinking the Court gave the President a free hand in wartime. These cases mostly turned on whether Congress had authorized the action and on the Constitution's procedural protections (due process, habeas corpus). Check what Congress had said before reading the holding.

blocks.html: The President is the head of a branch, not above the law, but the Constitution's structure gives the office some special protections. Two kinds of questions recur: executive privilege (may the President keep communications confidential?) and immunity (may the President be sued or prosecuted?). The answers depend on the kind of proceeding and the kind of act. Impeachment, the political remedy, is covered in Civics and Government.

opts.facts: A special prosecutor investigating the Watergate break-in subpoenaed tape recordings of conversations in President Nixon's office for use in the criminal trial of his aides. Nixon claimed an absolute executive privilege.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Burger, for a unanimous Court (Justice Rehnquist not participating): the privilege is real and rooted in the separation of powers, because Presidents need candid advice. But it is qualified. A generalized claim of confidentiality must yield to the demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial. The courts, not the President, decide.
opts.later: Nixon released the tapes and resigned on August 9, 1974, about two weeks later.

Holding

blocks.html: The cases balance two principles. One is that no one is above the law: courts need evidence, and people harmed by unofficial conduct deserve a remedy. The other is that the Constitution vests the executive power in a single President who must be able to act decisively, which personal liability for official decisions could chill. Where an act is official and the proceeding would intrude on the core of the office, protection is strongest; where the act is unofficial, it is weakest.

United States v. Nixon (1974): executive privilege is qualified and yields to a criminal trial's need for evidence. Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982): absolute civil immunity for official acts. Clinton v. Jones (1997): no immunity from civil suits about unofficial acts.

blocks.title: Official or unofficial?
blocks.q: A former President is sued for damages by a federal employee who says she was fired from her government job in retaliation for testifying to Congress. The firing was done through the normal chain of command. Which precedent controls?
steps: Proceeding: civil damages suit.
Act: a personnel decision within the "outer perimeter" of official duties.
Nixon v. Fitzgerald gave absolute civil immunity for such acts; the facts are close to Fitzgerald's own.
blocks.a: Nixon v. Fitzgerald: the suit is barred. Other remedies remain, such as impeachment and congressional oversight, which the Court mentioned.

blocks.title: Sorting a new case
blocks.q: A former President is sued by a private person for damages over something he did as a candidate, before taking office. Which precedent controls?
steps: Proceeding: civil damages suit.
Act: unofficial, before office.
Clinton v. Jones: no immunity for unofficial acts; the suit can proceed.
blocks.a: Clinton v. Jones. Nixon v. Fitzgerald would apply only to official acts.

blocks.html: Mixing up civil and criminal immunity, or official and unofficial acts. Sort each case by the kind of proceeding (civil or criminal) and the kind of act (official or unofficial) before stating the rule. Check the table above.

Hamilton contrasted the President with the British king in Federalist No. 69, noting that the President would be "liable to prosecution and punishment in the ordinary course of law" after removal by impeachment. Both sides of the immunity debate cite that passage.

blocks.html: After the turn of 1937, the Court stopped second-guessing economic legislation. That change produced a standard of review that now applies to most laws challenged under the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses: rational basis review. It is the bottom tier of a three-tier framework you will use throughout Constitutional Law II.

opts.facts: The Filled Milk Act of 1923 banned interstate shipment of "filled milk," skimmed milk mixed with vegetable oil instead of milk fat. Carolene Products was indicted for shipping it.
opts.reasoning: Justice Stone: economic regulation is presumed constitutional; it will be upheld if it rests on a rational basis within the knowledge and experience of legislators. Congress had evidence that filled milk was nutritionally inferior and could be passed off as whole milk.
opts.later: Footnote four suggested that courts might apply closer review to laws that fall within specific prohibitions of the Constitution (such as the Bill of Rights), that restrict the political processes, or that are directed at "discrete and insular minorities."

blocks.html: Why so deferential? Courts are not elected and are poorly placed to weigh economic and social policy. The Lochner era (see Constitutional Law II) showed what happens when judges strike down economic laws they find unwise. Rational basis leaves those choices to legislatures, which voters can change. Footnote four explains when that trust breaks down: when the political process itself is blocked, or when a group cannot protect itself through it, closer review makes sense.

Most laws get rational basis review: a law is upheld if it is rationally related to a legitimate government interest. Any conceivable legitimate reason will do, and the challenger must negate every conceivable basis (Williamson v. Lee Optical, 1955). Carolene Products (1938) and its footnote four suggested closer review for some laws.

opts.facts: Oklahoma barred opticians from fitting or replacing eyeglass lenses without a prescription from an optometrist or ophthalmologist, even to copy existing lenses into new frames.
opts.reasoning: The unanimous Court: the law may have been needless and wasteful in many cases, but it is for the legislature, not the courts, to balance the advantages and disadvantages. The legislature might have concluded that frequent eye exams were needed to detect disease. A conceivable rational reason was enough.

blocks.title: Rational basis in action
blocks.q: A city bans food trucks within 300 feet of restaurants. A food truck owner says the law only protects restaurants from competition. Apply rational basis.
steps: Is there a legitimate interest? Conceivable ones: traffic and pedestrian safety near busy restaurants, reducing congestion, sanitation.
Is the law rationally related to it? Keeping trucks away from crowded areas plausibly reduces congestion.
The city need not prove these were its actual reasons; the owner must negate every conceivable one.
blocks.a: Likely upheld under federal rational basis review, though the owner may argue that bare economic protectionism is not legitimate. (State constitutions sometimes require more.)

blocks.title: Rational basis "with bite"
blocks.q: In a few cases the Court struck down laws under rational basis. What do they have in common?
steps: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center (1985): a city denied a permit for a group home for people with intellectual disabilities; the Court found the denial rested on irrational prejudice.
Romer v. Evans (1996): a state constitutional amendment barring local protections for gay people was found to lack any rational relation to a legitimate purpose.
In both, the Court found the law's real basis was animus toward a group, and a bare desire to harm a group is not a legitimate interest.
blocks.a: Animus. Scholars call this "rational basis with bite"; the Court has not named it a separate tier.

blocks.html: Thinking the government must prove its actual reason under rational basis. Any conceivable legitimate reason will do, even one the legislature never stated, and the burden is on the challenger. Check: can you imagine any legitimate reason the law might serve? If so, it almost always survives.

blocks.html: Rational basis defers to the government. For some laws, the Court demands more. Two higher tiers developed after footnote four: strict scrutiny and intermediate scrutiny. Each has two parts: how important the government's goal must be (the interest) and how closely the law must fit it (the fit). Learn them as pairs.

blocks.html: Why have tiers at all? Each tier sets how much the Court trusts the political process for a type of law. Where a law classifies by race, or burdens a fundamental right, history shows the political process often fails, so the government must justify the law with a compelling reason and a close fit. Where a law classifies by sex, the Court found that stereotypes had long shaped law, but that some real differences may justify distinctions, so it chose a middle tier. The tiers make results more predictable than case-by-case balancing, though critics say they are too rigid or too open to manipulation.

Intermediate scrutiny requires an important government interest and means substantially related to it. Strict scrutiny requires a compelling interest and means narrowly tailored (often, the least restrictive means), with the burden on the government.

opts.facts: Oklahoma let women buy 3.2 percent beer at 18 but men only at 21. The state pointed to statistics showing young men were arrested for drunk driving more often.
opts.reasoning: Justice Brennan announced the intermediate test: classifications by sex "must serve important governmental objectives and must be substantially related to achievement of those objectives." Traffic safety was important, but the statistics (a small percentage of young men) showed too weak a relationship to justify the line.

blocks.title: Matching interest and fit
blocks.q: A state law gives a benefit to one group and not another. The state says its goal is "saving money" and the law is "reasonable." Which tier could that justification satisfy?
steps: Saving money is a legitimate interest; courts rarely treat it as important or compelling by itself.
"Reasonable" describes a rational relation, not substantial relation or narrow tailoring.
So the justification fits rational basis only.
blocks.a: Only rational basis. If the law triggers a higher tier, this justification will likely fail.

blocks.title: Narrow tailoring
blocks.q: A city, wanting to reduce noise (assume a compelling interest for the exercise), bans all speech in public parks. Is the ban narrowly tailored?
steps: Narrow tailoring asks whether the means are no broader than needed.
A total ban sweeps in quiet speech that causes no noise.
Less restrictive means exist: decibel limits, quiet hours.
blocks.a: No. Even a compelling interest cannot save a measure that is far broader than the problem. (Speech cases have their own rules, covered in Constitutional Law II.)

blocks.html: Mixing up the interest and the fit at each tier. Learn them as pairs: legitimate and rational; important and substantially related; compelling and narrowly tailored. Check that your answer names both parts of the same tier.

Strict scrutiny is often called "strict in theory, fatal in fact," but the Court has said that is not always so; some laws survive it. You will apply these tiers to race in Race and Strict Scrutiny and to sex in Sex Discrimination.

blocks.html: You know the three tiers. The hardest step in practice comes first: deciding which tier applies. The answer depends on what the law classifies (for equal protection) or what right it burdens (for due process and specific rights), not on how fair or unfair the law seems.

blocks.html: Why tie the tier to the classification rather than to the law's fairness? Because the point of the tiers is to decide how much to trust the legislature before looking at the merits. Race classifications get strict scrutiny because the Fourteenth Amendment's core purpose was to end official racial discrimination; the Court has applied strict scrutiny to all racial classifications, including those meant to help. A judge who chose the tier by asking "Is this law unfair?" would be deciding the case first and the standard second.

The tier depends on what the law classifies or burdens: race, national origin and fundamental rights trigger strict scrutiny; sex and legitimacy intermediate; most economic and social laws rational basis. Some areas use other tests instead of the tiers, such as the Mathews balance for procedural due process. Since 2022 the Court has judged Second Amendment and Establishment Clause cases by history and tradition rather than by the tiers.

blocks.title: Sorting three laws
blocks.q: Which tier applies? (a) A state law sets a mandatory retirement age of 65 for state police. (b) A city ordinance gives contracts preferences based on the race of business owners. (c) A state law sets different ages for men and women to serve on juries.
steps: (a) Age: rational basis.
(b) Race: strict scrutiny, even though the program is meant to help (Croson, 1989; Adarand, 1995).
(c) Sex: intermediate scrutiny, with an exceedingly persuasive justification required.
blocks.a: (a) rational basis, (b) strict, (c) intermediate.

blocks.title: When the tiers do not apply
blocks.q: A federal agency stops a person's disability benefits after reviewing medical reports, without first holding a hearing; a full hearing is available afterward. The person says due process required a hearing first. Which framework does the Court use?
steps: The claim is not that the law classifies anyone or burdens a fundamental right; it is about what procedures are owed before the government takes away a benefit.

For that question the Court uses the balance from Mathews v. Eldridge (1976): the private interest at stake, the risk of error under the current procedures and the value of more safeguards, and the government's interest, including cost.
In Mathews itself, the Court held that a hearing after the benefits stopped was enough.
blocks.a: A balancing test, not a tier.

blocks.html: Applying strict scrutiny to any law that seems unfair. First identify the classification or right; the tier follows from that, not from the law's wisdom. A harsh economic law still gets rational basis; a well-meant racial classification still gets strict scrutiny. Check: what does the law classify by, or which right does it burden?

Justices disagree about the framework itself. Some argue the tiers are judge-made and should give way to text and history in more areas; others argue that history-based tests are hard to apply and that the tiers give needed structure. Practice here asks which test applies, not which approach is better. The framework continues in Constitutional Law II, including the Second Amendment and the Establishment Clause tests.
